legend: On his voyage to hunt the elusive white whale, Captain Ahab is swamped with tasks to do during day-to-day life on his ship. The good news is that he has the life-sustaining power of coffee on his side. The bad news is that there is a limited amount of coffee in his ship's hold. There are $$$n$$$ days, each with some amount of work $$$w_i$$$ to do. Each unit of work costs 1 energy, and every day starts with 0 energy.

There are $$$m$$$ cups of coffee that can be drunk on any day. The first coffee drunk on any day gives $$$k$$$ energy, the second gives $$$k-1$$$ energy, and so on, until the $$$k^{th}$$$ coffee gives $$$1$$$ energy; any coffee drunk afterward gives no energy.
Ahab needs your help to ration his coffee to complete as much work as possible.
input: The first line of input contains $$$n$$$, $$$m$$$, and $$$k$$$ ($$$1 \le n \le 10^5, 1 \le m, k \le 10^9$$$), the number of days, cups of coffee, and initial energy from coffee, respectively.
The second line contains $$$n$$$ integers, $$$w_1, w_2, ..., w_n$$$ ($$$1 \le w_i \le 10^{18}$$$), the amount of work to be done each day.
output: The output should be one line containing the maximum possible amount of work that can be done.
note: It is optimal for Ahab to drink two coffees on the first day, one on the second day, and one on the third day for $$$5+2+3 = 10$$$ units of work total.

legend.ai: 在追捕难以捉摸的白鲸的航程中，亚哈船长在船上的日常生活里被各种任务压得喘不过气。好消息是他有维系生命的咖啡之力相助。坏消息是船上货舱里的咖啡数量有限。一共有 $$$n$$$ 天，每天都有一定量的工作 $$$w_i$$$ 要做。每单位工作消耗 1 点能量，且每天开始时能量为 0。
有 $$$m$$$ 杯咖啡，可以在任意一天饮用。在任意一天喝的第一杯咖啡提供 $$$k$$$ 点能量，第二杯提供 $$$k-1$$$ 点能量，以此类推，直到第 $$$k^{th}$$$ 杯咖啡提供 $$$1$$$ 点能量；此后喝的咖啡不提供能量。
Ahab 需要你的帮助来ration他的咖啡，以完成尽可能多的工作。

input.ai: 输入第一行包含 $$$n$$$、$$$m$$$ 和 $$$k$$$($$$1 \le n \le 10^5, 1 \le m, k \le 10^9$$$)，分别表示天数、咖啡杯数以及从咖啡中获得的初始能量。
第二行包含 $$$n$$$ 个整数，$$$w_1, w_2, ..., w_n$$$ ($$$1 \le w_i \le 10^{18}$$$)，表示每天需要完成的工作量。

output.ai: 输出应为一行，包含可以完成的最大可能工作量。

note.ai: Ahab 最优的做法是在第一天喝两杯咖啡，第二天喝一杯，第三天喝一杯，总共完成 $$$5+2+3 = 10$$$ 单位的工作。

legend: This is the hard version of the problem. The difference between the versions is that in this version, the path may end in any cave.
Henry went on an expedition into a network of caves in search of ancient artifacts. The entrance to the caves is at vertex 1%%ZSMJ0%%, and the corridors between caves form a tree.
Henry lights his way with a magic lamp. To pass through the i%%ZSMJ1%%-th corridor, the lamp spends wi%%ZSMJ2%% units of charge each time it is traversed.

However, the cave corridors are extremely unstable. After two traversals of the same corridor, its vault becomes too fragile, and it is impossible to use this corridor a third time. Therefore, Henry may traverse each corridor at most twice, regardless of the direction of movement.

There is an artifact in every cave. On the first visit to vertex v%%ZSMJ3%%, the artifact changes the lamp charge by av%%ZSMJ4%% units: some artifacts restore charge (those with av>0%%ZSMJ5%%), while others are cursed and instead take it away (av<0%%ZSMJ6%%). Visiting the cave again has no effect on the lamp charge.
At the beginning of the expedition, Henry is in cave 1%%ZSMJ7%% and immediately activates the artifact there. The lamp charge must never become negative at any moment.
Henry must visit all caves and collect all artifacts. After that, he can activate a portal in any cave and leave the dungeon, so he does not need to return to the entrance.
Determine the minimum initial lamp charge with which Henry can complete the expedition.
input: The first line contains one integer n%%ZSMJ8%% (1≤n≤2⋅105)%%ZSMJ9%% — the number of caves.

The second line contains n%%ZSMJ10%% integers a1,a2,…,an%%ZSMJ11%% (−109≤ai≤109)%%ZSMJ12%% — the changes in lamp charge after the first visit to the corresponding caves. Note that each corridor can be traversed at most twice, regardless of direction.

The next n−1%%ZSMJ13%% lines contain three integers each: ui%%ZSMJ14%%, vi%%ZSMJ15%%, and wi%%ZSMJ16%% (1≤ui,vi≤n, ui≠vi, 1≤wi≤109)%%ZSMJ17%% — the endpoints of the i%%ZSMJ18%%-th corridor and the amount of charge required to traverse it.
It is guaranteed that the corridors form a tree.
output: Print one integer — the minimum initial lamp charge with which Henry can visit all caves without the lamp charge ever becoming negative.

legend.ai: 这是本题的困难版本。两个版本的区别在于，在这个版本中，路径可以终止于任意洞穴。
Henry 深入一个洞穴网络探险，寻找古代文物。洞穴入口位于顶点 1%%ZSMJ0%%，洞穴之间的通道构成一棵树。
Henry用魔法灯照亮前路。穿过第 i%%ZSMJ1%% 条走廊时，灯每次都会消耗 wi%%ZSMJ2%% 单位电量。
然而，洞穴的通道极其不稳定。同一条通道在被经过两次后，其拱顶就会变得过于脆弱，无法第三次使用这条通道。因此，无论移动方向如何，Henry 最多只能经过每条通道两次。
每个洞穴中都有一个神器。第一次访问顶点 v%%ZSMJ3%% 时，神器会使灯的电量变化 av%%ZSMJ4%% 个单位：有些神器会恢复电量（那些 av>0%%ZSMJ5%% 的），而另一些则被诅咒，反而会消耗电量（av<0%%ZSMJ6%%）。再次访问该洞穴对灯的电量没有影响。
探险开始时，Henry 位于洞穴 1%%ZSMJ7%%，并立即激活了那里的神器。灯的充能值在任何时刻都绝不能变为负数。
Henry必须访问所有洞穴并收集所有神器。之后，他可以在任意洞穴中激活传送门并离开地牢，因此他无需返回入口。
求出 Henry 完成探险所需的最小初始提灯电量。

input.ai: 第一行包含一个整数 n%%ZSMJ8%% (1≤n≤2⋅105)%%ZSMJ9%% —— 洞穴的数量。
第二行包含 n%%ZSMJ10%% 个整数 a1,a2,…,an%%ZSMJ11%% (−109≤ai≤109)%%ZSMJ12%%——首次访问对应洞穴后灯的电量变化量。注意，每条走廊无论方向最多只能经过两次。
接下来的 n−1%%ZSMJ13%% 行每行包含三个整数：ui%%ZSMJ14%%、vi%%ZSMJ15%% 和 wi%%ZSMJ16%%（1≤ui,vi≤n, ui≠vi, 1≤wi≤109）%%ZSMJ17%% —— 第 i%%ZSMJ18%% 条走廊的两个端点以及通过它所需的电量。
保证走廊构成一棵树。

output.ai: 输出一个整数——亨利能够访问所有洞穴且灯的电量始终不会变为负数所需的最小初始电量。

legend: A recently published book receives readers' ratings on a scale from $$$1$$$ to $$$n$$$. Readers leave reviews one by one, and at any moment the book's rating is the arithmetic mean of all ratings given so far.
For each reader, their type $$$t_i$$$ and desired rating $$$x_i$$$ are known.
If $$$t_i = \texttt{S}$$$, then the reader always gives the book rating $$$x_i$$$.

If $$$t_i = \texttt{D}$$$, then before voting the reader sees the current rating of the book and the number of readers who have already voted. Then they choose an integer rating from $$$1$$$ to $$$n$$$ so that the book's rating after their vote is as close as possible to $$$x_i$$$.
The organizers may choose any order in which the readers leave their reviews.
$$$\texttt{Andrew-13}$$$ became interested in the minimum and maximum possible final ratings of the book. Find these values.
input: The first line of the input contains 2 integers $$$n, m$$$ $$$(1 \le n, m \le 2 \cdot 10^5)$$$ — the maximum possible rating of the book and the number of readers, respectively.

Each of the next $$$m$$$ lines contains a character $$$t_i$$$ ($$$t_i = \texttt{S}$$$ or $$$t_i = \texttt{D}$$$) and an integer $$$x_i$$$ $$$(1 \le x_i \le n)$$$ — the reader type and their desired rating.

The character $$$t_i$$$ is $$$\texttt{S}$$$ if the reader always gives rating $$$x_i$$$, or $$$\texttt{D}$$$ if the reader chooses a rating so that the final rating after their vote is as close as possible to $$$x_i$$$.
output: Print two numbers in a single line — the minimum and maximum possible final ratings of the book.
Your answer will be considered correct if its absolute or relative error does not exceed $$$10^{-9}$$$.
Formally, let your answer be $$$a$$$, and the jury's answer be $$$b$$$. Your answer is considered correct if $$$\frac{|a - b|}{\max(1, |b|)} \le 10^{-9}$$$.

legend: There are $$$n$$$ collectible cards arranged in a fixed order on a strip. The $$$i$$$-th card has type number $$$a_i$$$.
The strip can be cut between some adjacent cards, obtaining several non-empty sets. The order of the cards cannot be changed, so each set consists of some contiguous fragment of the strip.

For a set of cards, define its $$$\operatorname{MEX}$$$ as the minimum non-negative type number that does not appear among the cards in that set. For example, $$$\operatorname{MEX}([0, 3, 2, 2, 0]) = 1$$$, and $$$\operatorname{MEX}([1, 2, 6]) = 0$$$.
A set is called $$$\texttt{valid}$$$ if its $$$\operatorname{MEX}$$$ lies in the range from $$$L$$$ to $$$R$$$ inclusive.
Find the number of ways to cut the strip so that all resulting sets are $$$\texttt{valid}$$$. Since the answer may be large, output it modulo $$$998244353$$$.
input: The first line of the input contains three integers $$$n$$$, $$$L$$$, and $$$R$$$ $$$(1 \le n \le 5 \cdot 10^5,\ 0 \le L \le R \le n)$$$ — the number of cards and the bounds of the valid values of $$$\operatorname{MEX}$$$.
The second line contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$$$ $$$(0 \le a_i \le n)$$$ — the type numbers of the cards on the strip.
output: Print one number in a single line — the number of ways to cut the strip modulo $$$998244353$$$.

problems.hint: Conditions.

legend: Barbara has a garden, represented as an $$$n \times n$$$ grid. She has bought $$$n^2$$$ slabstones indexed from $$$1$$$ to $$$n^2$$$ and placed them in her garden, so she can enjoy stepping slabstones from one to another every day. The slabstones are arranged in row-major order, that is, the slabstone at cell $$$(i, j)$$$ is indexed $$$(i - 1) \times n + j$$$.

Barbara would like to redesign her garden, so she invited Babara, a famous interior designer. After careful consideration, Barbara suggests that the slabstone at cell $$$(i, j)$$$ should be indexed $$$a_{ij}$$$. They will use the following "elegant" process to rearrange the slabstones:
Color each slabstone either red or blue.
Shift the red slabstones within each row (so they can only move left or right).
Shift the blue slabstones within each column (so they can only move up or down).

However, there is an important restriction: Any two slabstones with the same color should remain non-overlapping during the rearrangement of the slabstones. Note that a red slabstone and a blue slabstone can temporarily overlap (but in order to have the desired garden, they should not overlap at the end).
Now Barbara wants to know whether they can rearrange the slabstones as desired.
input: The first line contains an integer $$$n$$$, representing the size of the garden.
Followed by $$$n$$$ lines, the $$$i$$$-th of which contains $$$n$$$ integers, the $$$j$$$-th integer $$$a_{ij}$$$ represents the index of the slabstone at cell $$$(i, j)$$$ in the desired garden.
$$$1 \leq a_{ij} \leq n^2$$$
All $$$a_{ij}$$$ are distinct.
output: If the slabstones can be rearranged as desired, output Yes; otherwise output No.
note: Explanation for Sample 1

Below is the illustration of one possible way to rearrange the slabstones. The blue slabstones in step 2 (and the red slabstones in step 3) are hidden for clarity. The slabstones should be shifted in some order that does not violate the restriction. For example, in step 3, you can shift slabstone $$$9$$$ one cell down then shift slabstone $$$5$$$ one cell down, but not in the opposite order.

legend: Madoka was originally an ordinary student who went to school happily every day. However, one day she was suddenly persuaded to become a magical girl, and thus began her endless battles against enemies to protect the world.

The transportation network of this world is shaped like a complete $$$k$$$-ary tree with $$$l$$$ levels. Her base is located in Central City, which is located at the root node (level $$$1$$$), and all enemies lurk at the leaves (level $$$l$$$). Every non-leaf node has exactly $$$k$$$ children, which are ordered from left to right as its $$$1$$$-st, $$$2$$$-nd, $$$\dots$$$, $$$k$$$-th child, exactly as they are drawn in the picture below. Given $$$k$$$ and $$$l$$$, we can determine the total number of nodes in the tree (denoted $$$S$$$), which is at most $$$10^6$$$. Below is an example transportation network with $$$k = 3$$$ and $$$l = 4$$$, where $$$S=40$$$:
![](https://espresso.codeforces.com/703283f7724c5649755c9157c5e187a78427fdb5.png)
Over time, Madoka has already completed $$$n$$$ enemy extermination missions sequentially. For each mission, she started her journey from Central City.

However, the enemies are not the only threat. There exists a special kind of mysterious "white rabbit" in this world that Madoka finds extremely annoying and difficult to deal with. To conserve her precious magical energy for the actual battles, Madoka actively chooses which enemy to hunt based on the safest route. She evaluates the routes to all leaves and always selects a root-to-leaf path that contains the minimum total number of white rabbits along the way.

Several different paths may share this minimum total, so Madoka fixes her route in the following deterministic way. She walks down from the root one node at a time. Standing at a non-leaf node $$$v$$$, she looks at every child $$$c$$$ of $$$v$$$ that keeps her on a path of the minimum total (that is, the number of white rabbits on the road from $$$v$$$ to $$$c$$$, plus the minimum number of white rabbits on a path from $$$c$$$ down to a leaf of $$$c$$$'s subtree, is as small as possible among all children of $$$v$$$), and she always steps into the leftmost such child, that is, the one with the smallest index among them. She repeats this until she arrives at a leaf.

Unfortunately, these white rabbits have a strange affinity for magical girls and are strongly attracted to Madoka's magical trail. After she completes the $$$i$$$-th mission, her residual magic instantly triggers a rapid multiplication of the creatures. Specifically, on every single road segment that Madoka just traveled across during that mission, the number of white rabbits permanently occupying that road increases by $$$w_i$$$. (Initially, the world was peaceful, and there were $$$0$$$ white rabbits on all roads.)

As the missions pile up, the network becomes increasingly congested with these white rabbits. Madoka needs to know how bad the situation has eventually become. Determine the total number of white rabbits Madoka will inevitably encounter on her chosen path during her NEXT ($$$n+1$$$)-th extermination mission.
input: The first line contains three integers $$$k$$$, $$$l$$$, and $$$n$$$, representing the branching factor of the tree, the number of levels, and the number of completed missions.
The second line contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$w_1, w_2, \dots, w_n$$$, representing the sequence of values by which the white rabbits increase on the traveled road segments after each mission.
$$$1 \leq n \leq 2 \times 10^5$$$
The total number of nodes in the tree does not exceed $$$10^6$$$.
output: Output a single integer representing the total number of white rabbits on the path Madoka will choose during her NEXT ($$$n+1$$$)-th mission.
note: Explanation for Sample 1

The tree has $$$4$$$ leaves, numbered $$$1$$$ to $$$4$$$ from left to right; leaves $$$1$$$ and $$$2$$$ belong to the root's $$$1$$$-st child, leaves $$$3$$$ and $$$4$$$ to its $$$2$$$-nd child. Over the five missions Madoka visited leaves $$$1$$$, $$$3$$$, $$$2$$$, $$$4$$$, $$$1$$$.

The first two missions are the ones that use the tie-breaking rule. In mission $$$1$$$, every road was still empty, so all four routes tied; she went into the left child at the root and again at the next node, reaching leaf $$$1$$$. In mission $$$2$$$, the four routes cost $$$2$$$, $$$1$$$, $$$0$$$, $$$0$$$: at the root the $$$2$$$-nd child was strictly better, and there its two leaves tied at $$$0$$$, so she took the leftmost of them, leaf $$$3$$$. In the remaining three missions, the route with the fewest white rabbits was unique: leaf $$$2$$$ at cost $$$1$$$, then leaf $$$4$$$ at cost $$$2$$$, then leaf $$$1$$$ at cost $$$5$$$.

After these $$$5$$$ missions, the four routes cost $$$15$$$, $$$12$$$, $$$8$$$ and $$$10$$$, respectively. Thus, for her next mission, Madoka takes the path to leaf $$$3$$$ and will inevitably encounter exactly $$$8$$$ white rabbits.

problems.hint: From island $1$ . Find the latest time to start from $i$ .

legend: In a tourist archipelago consisting of $$$n$$$ islands, there are $$$m$$$ bidirectional bridges connecting them. The islands are numbered $$$1, 2, \ldots, n$$$. The $$$i$$$-th bridge connects islands $$$u_i$$$ and $$$v_i$$$, and it takes $$$t_i$$$ minutes to cross. Furthermore, each bridge has a height $$$h_i$$$, representing its height above sea level in centimeters.

An unprecedented natural disaster has struck the archipelago, causing the sea level to rise at a rate of $$$1$$$ centimeter per minute. A bridge $$$i$$$ becomes unusable exactly $$$h_i$$$ minutes after the disaster begins. To ensure safety, a vehicle can only cross bridge $$$i$$$ if the entire traversal completes before the bridge is submerged. Specifically, if a vehicle starts crossing bridge $$$i$$$ at time $$$T$$$, it must arrive at the other end by time $$$T + t_i$$$, and this arrival time must satisfy $$$T + t_i \le h_i$$$.

Island $$$1$$$ serves as the evacuation center. Residents on each island are intelligent; they will choose a route that allows them to reach island $$$1$$$ safely before any bridge they cross becomes submerged. If no such path exists, they will remain on their current island to await rescue.
Given this scenario, for each island $$$k$$$ (where $$$k \in \{1, \ldots, n\}$$$), determine if the residents on island $$$k$$$ can safely reach island $$$1$$$.
input: The first line contains two integers $$$n$$$ and $$$m$$$, representing the number of islands and the number of bridges, respectively.

Followed by $$$m$$$ lines, the $$$i$$$-th of which contains four integers $$$u_i, v_i, t_i, h_i$$$, representing a bridge connecting islands $$$u_i$$$ and $$$v_i$$$ with travel time $$$t_i$$$ and height $$$h_i$$$.
$$$1\leq m\leq 3\times 10^5$$$
$$$1\leq u_i, v_i \leq n, u_i\neq v_i$$$
$$$1\leq t_i \leq h_i \leq 10^9$$$
output: Output a single string of length $$$n$$$. The $$$i$$$-th character of the string should be '1' if the residents of island $$$i$$$ can safely reach island $$$1$$$, and '0' otherwise.
note: Explanation for Sample 1

Residents of island $$$1$$$ are already at island $$$1$$$. Residents of island $$$3$$$ can safely cross the first bridge and arrive at island $$$1$$$ at time $$$2$$$. However, residents of island $$$2$$$ must first cross the second bridge to reach island $$$3$$$ at time $$$3$$$; if they then attempt to cross the first bridge, they will get stuck in the middle at time $$$4$$$, exactly when the bridge becomes unusable since $$$h_1=4$$$. Therefore, the residents of island $$$2$$$ cannot safely reach island $$$1$$$.

problems.hint: Hall's theorem. And find the lexicographically minimum order of feasible $s$ .

legend: Class leader A-Ming is arranging the $$$n$$$ students of his class into a single row to take a graduation photo. The $$$n$$$ students all have distinct heights, and A-Ming holds a roster listing the real height of every student.

The students were already standing in some order. For fun, A-Ming handed each student a slip of paper and asked everyone to look to their right and compute one number: how many of the people standing behind them (i.e. to the right in the row) are shorter than they are? Everyone wrote down their number and handed the slip back. The slips were originally collected in left-to-right order of the row (the first slip belongs to the student standing first, and so on).

Then a sudden gust of wind scattered all the slips on the ground! A-Ming gathered them back up, but their order was completely lost, leaving only an unordered collection of numbers $$$s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_n$$$.
The photographer is about to arrive and everyone has run off to play. A-Ming is left holding only the height roster and the shuffled pile of slips.

Help A-Ming decide: is it possible to reconstruct at least one valid standing order consistent with the numbers on the slips? If so, to make the picture look as harmonious as possible, output the lexicographically smallest height arrangement among all valid orders (placing shorter students as far toward the front as possible). If the numbers cannot fit together at all, output -1.
input: The first line contains a single integer $$$n$$$, representing the number of students.
The second line contains $$$n$$$ distinct integers $$$h_1, h_2, \ldots, h_n$$$, representing the real heights of the students.
The third line contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_n$$$, representing the shuffled collection of numbers written on the slips.
$$$1 \leq n \leq 2 \times 10^5$$$
$$$1 \leq h_i \leq 10^9$$$, and all $$$h_i$$$ are distinct.
$$$0 \leq s_i  \lt  n$$$
output: If a valid standing order exists, output a single line of $$$n$$$ integers: the lexicographically smallest valid sequence of heights, separated by single spaces.
If no valid standing order exists, output a single line containing -1.
note: Explanation for Sample 1

The slips form the multiset $$$\{0, 0, 1\}$$$. Two standing orders are consistent with it: heights $$$[10, 30, 20]$$$ (slip values $$$0, 1, 0$$$) and $$$[20, 10, 30]$$$ (slip values $$$1, 0, 0$$$). The first is lexicographically smaller, so the answer is $$$10\ 30\ 20$$$.
Explanation for Sample 2
With two students, the person standing last has nobody to their right, so one slip must read $$$0$$$. Both slips read $$$1$$$, which is impossible, so the answer is $$$-1$$$.

legend: Dzy and Fox have a sequence A consisting of N numbers [A1...AN]. Dzy starts by taking the first number, then Fox takes the second number, then Dzy takes the third number and so on, they continue taking turns until all of the N numbers are taken. The player with the highest sum of numbers wins.
Since Dzy is your dear friend, you decided to rotate the sequence (you may rotate it as many times as you like) in order to maximize Dzy's sum of numbers.
Rotation is defined as removing the first element from the beginning of the sequence and adding it to the end of the sequence.
So given the sequence A , you have to help Dzy and let him achieve the maximum possible sum.

output: Output T lines , The answer for each testcase which is the maximum achievable sum by Dzy if you help him.

legend: Since the 2017 world finals will be in Rapid City, South Dakota, the MaratonIME's coach decides to visit the city to know the contest location.

The city is preparing to receive the best computer programmers in the world. To ensure the safety of the event, metal detectors are being installed at the entrance of the convention center where the contest will be held. To avoid long waits in the line, the security officers were instructed to send every person that activates the metal detector to the end of the line.

The coach noticed that one of the metal detectors is defective and it is always activated alternately. This means that the first person does not activate it and the next person does. The third person does not activate it and the next person does, and so on.
Given that there are N people in the line, the coach, that is the i-th in the line, wants to know when he will be able to go through the metal detector without activating it.
input: The input starts with an integer T, the number of test cases.
Each test case consists of two integers, N and i, corresponding to the number of people in the line and the position of the coach in the line, respectively.
Limits
1 ≤ i ≤ N
output: For each test case, print a line with one integer j meaning that the coach will be the j-th person to go through the metal detector without activating it.

statement.title: D. Domain Expansion Abraham échate un hint

legend: Rem, Alex, José, and Abraham are spending the weekend exploring La Plata in the middle of the Training Camp Argentina. During their trip, they decide to visit an attraction called La República de los Pibitos.

The attraction consists of $$$n$$$ locations, numbered from $$$1$$$ to $$$n$$$. From each location, there is exactly one path leading to another location. Therefore, La República de los Pibitos can be represented as a functional graph: every vertex has exactly one outgoing edge.

The graph is connected if the directions of the edges are ignored. Consequently, it contains exactly one directed cycle. Finding this cycle is one of the main attractions of La República de los Pibitos.

Abraham has already seen the map and knows which locations belong to the cycle. However, Rem, Alex, and José have not. Instead of showing them the map, Abraham challenges them to determine all the vertices of the cycle using at most $$$3n$$$ hints.

For each hint, they may choose two integers $$$u$$$ and $$$k$$$ ($$$1 \le u \le n$$$, $$$1 \le k \le n$$$). Starting at vertex $$$u$$$, consider the sequence of vertices visited while following the unique outgoing edge exactly $$$k$$$ times. Thus, the sequence contains the starting vertex and the $$$k$$$ vertices reached after each step.
Abraham will answer whether some vertex appears more than once in this sequence, or whether all visited vertices are distinct.
Using at most $$$3n$$$ such hints, Rem, Alex, and José must determine exactly which vertices belong to the unique directed cycle of La República de los Pibitos.
input: The input contains a single integer $$$n$$$ ($$$1 \le n \le 10^4$$$) — the number of vertices in the functional graph.
After reading $$$n$$$, the interaction starts.
You can ask Abraham at most $$$3n$$$ hints.

To ask a hint, output a line in the following format: "? $$$u$$$ $$$k$$$", where $$$u$$$ is the starting vertex and $$$k$$$ ($$$1 \le k \le n$$$) is the number of edges that will be traversed by repeatedly following the unique outgoing edge.
After each hint, the evaluator will provide a single line containing:
"Yes", if some vertex is visited more than once among the starting vertex and the $$$k$$$ vertices reached after each step;
"No", if all these $$$k+1$$$ visited vertices are distinct.

Once you have determined all the vertices that belong to the unique directed cycle, output a line in the following format: "! $$$m$$$ $$$v_1$$$ $$$v_2$$$ $$$\dots$$$ $$$v_m$$$", where $$$m$$$ is the number of vertices in the cycle and $$$v_1,v_2,\dots,v_m$$$ are exactly the vertices that belong to it, in any order.

The graph is guaranteed to be a connected functional graph, meaning every vertex has exactly one outgoing edge and the underlying undirected graph is connected. Therefore, the graph contains exactly one directed cycle.
After printing each line, do not forget to output the end of the line and flush the output buffer. Otherwise, you will receive the "Idleness limit exceeded" verdict. To flush, use:
"fflush(stdout)" or "cout.flush()" in C++;
"System.out.flush()" in Java;
"flush(output)" in Pascal;
"stdout.flush()" in Python.

The interactor is adaptive. This means that the functional graph is not necessarily fixed before the interaction starts. Instead, the interactor may determine the hidden graph based on the queries made by your program, as long as all answers given during the interaction are consistent with at least one connected functional graph.
note: The functional graph for this example is shown below:
![](https://espresso.codeforces.com/ee204a1316fb24c2e23a8549a0fffec4d6cd9037.png)
For the first hint, "? 4 3", starting from vertex $$$4$$$ and walking $$$3$$$ steps visits the vertices $$$4, 1, 2, 3$$$. Since all of them are different, the answer is "No".
For the second hint, "? 4 4", the visited vertices are $$$4, 1, 2, 3, 1$$$. Vertex $$$1$$$ is visited twice, so the answer is "Yes".
For the third hint, "? 1 2", the visited vertices are $$$1, 2, 3$$$. Since all of them are different, the answer is "No".
For the fourth hint, "? 1 3", the visited vertices are $$$1, 2, 3, 1$$$. Vertex $$$1$$$ is visited twice, so the answer is "Yes".
Finally, the vertices belonging to the unique directed cycle are $$$1$$$, $$$2$$$, and $$$3$$$. Therefore, a valid final answer is "! 3 1 3 2". The vertices of the cycle may be reported in any order.

problems.hint: If the radius is $r$ , what is the area.

legend: You are chilling during your vacations, simulating divs and playing lol, when Nijika asks you a strange question.

Suppose an island shaped like a convex polygon undergoes morphological dilation using a disk of radius $$$r$$$ (resulting in a uniform expansion in all directions). What is the minimum radius $$$r$$$ such that the island reaches an area of at least $$$k$$$?
Formally, you are asked to find the minimum radius $$$r$$$ such that the Minkowski sum of the Polygon $$$P$$$ and a disk $$$D$$$ of radius $$$r$$$ results in an area greater than or equal to $$$k$$$.
The first thing that crossed your mind was: "Am I invited to this island?"
The answer is a resounding no (bro?). Now, help Nijika with her homework.
![](https://espresso.codeforces.com/54f3395042a4f82cc480bfde996aca4a4a1c0140.png)
input: The first line contains a single integer $$$t$$$ $$$(1 \leq t \leq 10^4)$$$ — the number of test cases.

The first line of each test case contains two integers $$$n$$$ and $$$k$$$ $$$(3 \leq n \leq 2 \cdot 10^5 \text{ and } 1 \leq k \leq 10^{16})$$$ — the number of vertex of the polygon and the area expect reach.
The following $$$n$$$ lines will each contain two integers $$$x_i$$$ and $$$y_i$$$ $$$( x_i, y_i \leq |10^8|)$$$, representing the $$$i$$$ vertex of convex polygon.
Additional constraints on the input:
In one test case, all points are pairwise distinct. The total number of points across all test cases does not exceed $$$2 \cdot 10^5$$$.
output: Print one number per test case, each representing the time when the poly-p reach area $$$k_i$$$. Your answer will be considered correct if its absolute or relative error does not exceed $$$10^{-4}$$$.

legend: Dwik and his brother Samir both received scholarships from a famous university in India. Their father, Besher, wants to send some money with each of them.
Besher has n coins, the ith coin has a value of ai. He will distribute these coins between his two sons in n steps. In the ith step, he chooses whether to give the ith coin to Dwik or to Samir.

Let xi be the absolute difference between the sum of Dwik's and Samir's coins after the ith step. The unfairness factor of a distribution is max({x1, x2, ..., xn}). Besher wants to minimize the unfairness factor, can you help him?
input: The first line of the input consists of a single integer t, the number of test cases. Each test case consists of 2 lines:
The first line contains an integer n (1 ≤ n ≤ 100).
The second line contains n integers a1, a2, ..., an (1 ≤ ai ≤ 100).
output: Print t lines, ith line containing a single integer, the answer to the ith test case.
note: In the first sample test, besher has 5 coins (1, 2, 1, 4, 3), he can distribute them in the following way:
Step 1: Give the first coin to dwik , d = 1, s = 0  x1 = |1 - 0| = 1
Step 2: Give the second coin to samir, d = 1, s = 2  x2 = |1 - 2| = 1
Step 3: Give the third coin to samir, d = 1, s = 3  x3 = |1 - 3| = 2
Step 4: Give the fourth coin to dwik, d = 5, s = 3  x4 = |5 - 3| = 2
Step 5: Give the fifth coin to samir, d = 5, s = 6  x5 = |5 - 6| = 1

legend: Celi and Itzel decided to start their fitness journey. They bought matching outfits and trendy water bottles, but couldn't afford a personal trainer, so they turned to TikTok. There they found Coach Emily, whose main training philosophy is: "The gym isn't about how much weight you lift, but about the aura you radiate".
According to Coach Emily's philosophy:
There are $$$N$$$ different exercises, numbered from $$$1$$$ to $$$N$$$.
On each of the $$$Z$$$ training days, Celi and Itzel can choose to perform exactly one exercise or take a rest day.
If they choose to perform exercise $$$i$$$ on day $$$c$$$ of a consecutive streak of that same exercise:   If $$$c \le d_i$$$: they gain $$$+k_i$$$ aura points.
If $$$c  \gt  d_i$$$: they gain $$$+(k_i - x_i)$$$ aura points (the penalty $$$x_i$$$ applies for each consecutive day that exceeds the optimal limit $$$d_i$$$).
If they choose to rest, they gain $$$0$$$ aura points and any active streak is reset to $$$0$$$.
If they switch from exercise $$$i$$$ to a different exercise $$$j \ne i$$$, the streak for exercise $$$j$$$ starts at $$$1$$$.

Initially (before day 1), they have no active streak. Celi and Itzel want to know the maximum amount of aura points they can accumulate by the end of the $$$Z$$$ training days if they choose their daily activities optimally.
input: The first line contains two integers $$$N$$$ and $$$Z$$$ ($$$1 \le N \le 1000$$$, $$$1 \le Z \le 1000$$$), the number of available exercises and the total number of training days.

The following $$$N$$$ lines describe the exercises. The $$$i$$$-th line contains three integers $$$k_i$$$, $$$d_i$$$, and $$$x_i$$$ ($$$1 \le k_i \le 10^9$$$, $$$1 \le d_i \le 100$$$, $$$0 \le x_i \le 10^9$$$), representing the base aura points per day, the optimal consecutive days threshold, and the penalty per additional consecutive day, respectively.
It is guaranteed that $$$\sum_{i=1}^N d_i \le 5000$$$.
output: Print a single integer: the maximum amount of aura points that Celi and Itzel can accumulate over the $$$Z$$$ training days.

problems.hint: Under what condition is the outcome fixed?

legend: You are the host of a large tournament that will feature $$$k$$$ athletes. You have $$$n$$$ familiar athletes, and you want to invite some of them to participate in a tournament. For each athlete, you know their strength and endurance (let's denote the strength of the $$$i$$$-th athlete as $$$p_i$$$ and their endurance as $$$s_i$$$). The $$$j$$$-th athlete will definitely defeat the $$$i$$$-th athlete only if they are strictly stronger and more enduring (i.e., if $$$p_j  \gt  p_i$$$ and $$$s_j  \gt  s_i$$$); otherwise, either of them could win.

The tournament proceeds as follows: as long as there are at least two athletes remaining, a pair is formed from two randomly selected athletes who have not been eliminated, the winner stays in the tournament, and the loser is eliminated. This continues until a tournament winner is determined.

To make the tournament as spectacular and unpredictable as possible, you want to invite a set of exactly $$$k$$$ athletes such that the winner is not predetermined. In other words, for a fixed set of $$$k$$$ athletes and considering all possible outcomes of pairwise wins and losses, there will be at least two outcomes where tournament winners are different.
Before finalizing the tournament lineup, you want to determine how many suitable sets of exactly $$$k$$$ athletes exist.
input: The first line contains two integers $$$n$$$ and $$$k$$$ ($$$1 \le k \le n \le 5000$$$) — the number of athletes and the size of the tournament.
The second line contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$p_1, p_2, \dots, p_n$$$ ($$$1 \le p_i \le 10^9$$$); where the $$$i$$$-th integer represents the strength of the $$$i$$$-th athlete.
The third line contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$s_1, s_2, \dots, s_n$$$ ($$$1 \le s_i \le 10^9$$$); where the $$$i$$$-th integer represents the endurance of the $$$i$$$-th athlete.
output: In a single line, print a number — the amount of suitable sets of exactly $$$k$$$ athletes. Since the answer may be quite large, output it modulo $$$998\,244\,353$$$.

legend.caiyun: 你是一场大型锦标赛的主办方，这场锦标赛将邀请 $$$k$$$ 运动员参加。你认识 $$$n$$$ 运动员，你想邀请他们中的一些人参加锦标赛。对于每个运动员，你都知道他们的力量和耐力 (让我们将 $$$i$$$ 运动员的力量表示为 $$$p_i$$$，耐力表示为 $$$s_i$$$)。$$$j$$$ 运动员只有在严格意义上更强壮、更耐力的情况下 (即 $$$p_j  \gt  p_i$$$ 和 $$$s_j  \gt  s_i$$$) 才能确定击败 $$$i$$$ 运动员;否则，他们中的任何一个都可能获胜。

problems.hint: Reduce the minimum number of permutations each time.

legend: This is an interactive problem. Remember that your program must flush the output buffer every time after printing. To flush the output buffer, you can use fflush(stdout) in C++, system.out.flush() in Java, stdout.flush() in Python, or flush(output) in Pascal. If you are using another programming language, check its documentation for how to perform this operation.
Vasya claims that he has invented a sorting algorithm for an $$$n$$$-element array $$$a$$$ (where all elements are pairwise distinct) that makes less than $$$\lceil \log_2 (n!)\rceil$$$ comparisons!

Vasya will ask you no more than $$$\lceil \log_2 (n!)\rceil - 1$$$ queries of the form: compare elements $$$a_i$$$ and $$$a_j$$$. Vasya claims that these queries are sufficient to uniquely determine the permutation of the positions of the array $$$a$$$ from the smallest element to the largest: $$$\operatorname{ord}_1, \operatorname{ord}_2, \dots, \operatorname{ord}_n$$$. Your task is to find a permutation of positions that differs from Vasya's permutation but is consistent with all of Vasya's queries.
Interaction
Initially, the jury's program will send a single integer $$$n$$$ ($$$3 \le n \le 18$$$) — the size of the array.
Then, the jury's program will send no more than $$$\lceil \log_2 (n!)\rceil - 1$$$ queries in the following format:
For each query, your program must output < if $$$a_i  \lt  a_j$$$, and > otherwise.
After that, the jury's program will send its answer in the following format:
$$$!$$$ $$$\operatorname{ord}_1 \operatorname{ord}_2 \dots \operatorname{ord}_n$$$

In response, your program must output a permutation that differs from the jury's permutation and is consistent with all previous queries, in the same format. If there are multiple possible permutations, output any of them. Please pay attention that you should not output the array $$$a$$$!

If your answer is correct, the jury's program will send the string CORRECT on a separate line, indicating that you can terminate the program. If the answer is incorrect, the jury's program will send the string ERROR on a separate line.

If your program violates the format of the queries, the jury will respond with the string ERROR. In this case, your program should terminate immediately to receive a Wrong answer verdict. Otherwise, you may receive an arbitrary verdict because your solution will continue to read from a closed stream.
Remember to flush the output buffer every time you print something!
note: Note that spaces in the examples are added only for readability. When checking solutions, the interactor will not output empty lines.

legend: In ancient Egypt, the construction of the pyramids is surrounded by mystery. Many researchers consider that the technology necessary to build them wasn't available at the time, and suspect that the Egyptian had extraterrestrial help to build them.

An example of those mysteries are the "It-miha" numbers. In the Egyptian province of It-miha was found a stone engraved with a sequence of numbers. Apparently the numbers had no link, until Poincaré, in the end of the XIX century, conjectured that the numbers written on that stone were the 500 first numbers that have no perfect square divisors.

A perfect square is a number is a number that has an integer square root, like 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, etc. We say a number is free of perfect square divisors if it is not divisible by any perfect square greater than 1.

It may seem simple to us, today, to determine such numbers, but we must remember that in that time, more than 3500 years ago, even the number system was different, and it made any calculation very difficult.
The "It-miha" numbers are very frequent in pyramids construction. The base of the Quéops pyramid, for example, is 210 × 210 and its height is 105 meters. All its dimensions are "It-miha" numbers!!!
The first ten "It-miha" numbers are 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 10, 11, 13 and 14. Your task is to, given an integer N, determine the Nth "It-miha" number.
input: The first line has a single integer Q, the number of queries.
Each of the next Q lines has an integer N.

output: For each query, print the Nth "It-miha" number.

Michael's favorite artist, Jackson, has recently started releasing new songs at an unprecedented rate. Michael wants to collect a physical copy of every record this artist releases, but his collection is getting too big. He already knows how many songs the artist releases over the first $$$n$$$ days, and wonders how many records he will have to buy on day $$$k$$$ if he continues to purchase every record.

Michael uses the function $$$f(x)$$$ to estimate the number of records released on day $$$x$$$. Michael already knows $$$f(x)$$$ for $$$1 \leq x \leq n$$$ as mentioned above. To compute future estimates, Michael uses the formula

input: The first line of input contains two space-separated integers, $$$n$$$ ($$$1 \leq n \leq 50$$$) and $$$k$$$ ($$$1 \leq k \leq 10^{18}$$$) — the number of days where we already know how many records were released on that day, and the day we would like to estimate, respectively.

The second line of input contains $$$n$$$ space-separated integers, where the $$$i^\text{th}$$$ number is $$$f(i)$$$ ($$$1 \leq f(i) \leq 10^9$$$) — the number of records purchashed on the $$$i^\text{th}$$$ day.
output: Print a single integer $$$f(k) \bmod {10^9+7}$$$ — the estimate for the number of records purchased on day $$$k$$$.

legend: ![](https://espresso.codeforces.com/a3d26e8c4e753b22c7dc5e7d70f7411ed4876f89.png)

Technoblade has finally decided to take a vacation. He has decided to visit an extensive list of cities and has hired you to make a travel plan for him. For this, each city has been given an identifier: an integer from 1 to N, with 1 being Techno's hometown. In addition, you have noted all available trips, which can be represented by 3 integers $$$a_i, b_i, c_i$$$, representing a route from $$$a_i$$$ to $$$b_i$$$ that costs $$$c_i$$$ reais and can be taken in both directions.

Now it's up to you to decide in which order to visit the cities. This plan must start in the hometown (number 1) and end there. In addition, every city must be visited at least once, with repetitions allowed.

As Technoblade is on vacation, he is not so concerned about money, and any plan that has a cost less than or equal to $$$2$$$ times the cost of an optimal plan will be accepted. For example, if we treat this problem as a graph problem, we can have a case like the one below:
![](https://espresso.codeforces.com/26114dab4255e8b331c94d95d482c823337b2ccb.png)

Note that the plan with the lowest cost has a cost of $$$8$$$. $$$1 \rightarrow 2 \rightarrow 4 \rightarrow 3 \rightarrow 4 \rightarrow 5 \rightarrow 6 \rightarrow 5 \rightarrow 1$$$ is an example of a plan.
However, the plan $$$1 \rightarrow 2 \rightarrow 3 \rightarrow 4 \rightarrow 5 \rightarrow 6\rightarrow 5 \rightarrow 1$$$ has a cost of $$$16 \leq 2\cdot 8$$$, so it is also a valid plan.
input: The first line contains 2 integers $$$1 \leq N \leq 3 \cdot 10^5$$$ and $$$1 \leq M \leq 5 \cdot 10^5$$$, representing the number of cities and the number of routes. Followed by $$$M$$$ lines with 3 integers $$$a_i, b_i, c_i$$$ each. It is guaranteed that $$$1 \leq a_i , b_i \leq N$$$, $$$a_i \neq b_i$$$ and $$$1 \leq c_i \leq 10^{12}$$$. It is also guaranteed that it is possible to make a plan that visits every city by using the given routes.
output: Print on the first line the cost of your found plan. On the second line, print an integer $$$K$$$ representing the number of cities in your plan. Finally, print $$$K$$$ integers $$$1 \leq p_i \leq N$$$ representing the cities to be visited in the order of your plan. You must ensure that $$$p_1 = p_K = 1$$$ and that for every $$$1 \leq i  \lt  K$$$, there is a route from $$$p_i$$$ to $$$p_{i+1}$$$. Also, you must ensure that $$$K \leq 2 \cdot 10^6$$$. It is guaranteed that there is a valid plan with this many cities.

legend: Geo Ghaffar has become the boss and he didn't want to tell Da7doo7 "You're FIRED" so he told him "solve this problem or you're FIRED", knowing that Da7doo7 is bad at geometry. Of course Da7doo7 called you, his best friend, for help.

You are given $$$n$$$ distinct points in a $$$2D$$$ plane with integer coordinates. You will draw a finite circle in such a way it passes through the maximum number of points. Since you hate floating numbers, you only have to print this maximum number.
![](https://espresso.codeforces.com/37a5db087b92c0254de43488e007c9823b45beb7.png)
input: The first line of the input contains a single integer $$$T$$$ ($$$1 \le T \le 100$$$) representing the number of test cases.

For each test case, the first line contains a single integer $$$n$$$ ($$$2 \le n \le 200$$$) denoting the number of points. Each of the next $$$n$$$ lines contain two integers $$$x_i$$$ and $$$y_i$$$ ($$$-10^6 \le x_i, y_i \le 10^6$$$) — the coordinates of every point. It is guaranteed that the given points are distinct.
It is guaranteed that the sum of $$$n$$$ over all test cases does not exceed $$$200$$$.
output: For each test case, print the answer in a single line.

problems.hint: It seems that the digits in the middle part of the final number are the same.

legend: One day, Johnny thought of a non-negative integer $$$n$$$, but unfortunately, he thinks the number is too small.

To make the number bigger, Johnny decides to make the number a Texas-Sized Number. To find the Texas-Sized Number of $$$n$$$, Johnny must calculate $$$$$$n + 10 \cdot n + 100 \cdot n + 1000 \cdot n + ... + 10^{10^{10}} \cdot n.$$$$$$
However, because this number takes too long to calculate, Johnny is only interested in the most common digit in the Texas-Sized Number of $$$n$$$. Can you help him find this digit?
input: The first line contains one non-negative integer $$$n$$$ — the number that Johnny thought of. This integer can be up to $$$10^5$$$ digits long.
output: Output a single integer — the most common digit in the Texas-Sized Number of $$$n$$$. If there is a tie, output any most common digit.

legend: Thanos has an array whose length is a power of two. Before he sees it, every element is chosen independently and uniformly from the integers $$$1,2,\ldots,K$$$.
An array is sorted if it is nondecreasing. While the current array is not sorted, Thanos performs a snap:
with probability $$$1/2$$$, he keeps the left half and discards the right half;
with probability $$$1/2$$$, he keeps the right half and discards the left half.
All snap choices are independent of each other and of the initial array. After each snap, he checks the remaining array again. An array of length one is always sorted.
The initial length is $$$N=2^n$$$. Find the expected number of snaps, where the expectation is taken over both the random initial array and all snap choices.
input: The only line contains two integers $$$n$$$ and $$$K$$$ – the exponent of the initial length and the number of possible values. The value of $$$n$$$ is between 0 and 200000, inclusive, and $$$K$$$ is between 1 and 200000, inclusive.
It is guaranteed that $$$nK$$$ is at most 20000000.
output: Let the expected number of snaps be the rational number $$$p/q$$$, where $$$p$$$ and $$$q$$$ are coprime. Print the residue modulo 998244353 of the product of $$$p$$$ and $$$q^{-1}$$$, where $$$q^{-1}$$$ is the multiplicative inverse of $$$q$$$ modulo 998244353. It is guaranteed that this inverse exists.
note: For $$$n=1$$$ and $$$K=2$$$, the only unsorted initial array is $$$[2,1]$$$. It requires one snap, so the expectation is $$$1/4$$$.

legend: You are given a permutation $$$P = (P_1, P_2, \dots, P_N)$$$ of the integers from $$$1$$$ to $$$N$$$.

For a subarray $$$P[l \dots r] = (P_l, P_{l+1}, \dots, P_r)$$$ (where $$$1 \le l \le r \le N$$$), let us define its Value as follows: $$$$$$\text{Value}(l, r) = \text{Sum}(l, r) - \text{MEX}(l, r)$$$$$$
Where:
$$$\text{Sum}(l, r) = \sum_{k=l}^{r} P_k$$$
$$$\text{MEX}(l, r)$$$ is the smallest positive integer ($$$1, 2, 3, \dots$$$) that does not appear in the subarray $$$P[l \dots r]$$$.
We call a range 3afwey if its value is as large as possible. El 3afweya is calling ..., and you have to respond. Determine the value of the 3afwey range.

legend: How many specific orders do you know? Ascending order, descending order, order of ascending length, order of ascending polar angle... Let's have a look at another specific order: d-sorting. This sorting is applied to the strings of length at least d, where d is some positive integer. The characters of the string are sorted in following manner: first come all the 0-th characters of the initial string, then the 1-st ones, then the 2-nd ones and so on, in the end go all the (d - 1)-th characters of the initial string. By the i-th characters we mean all the character whose positions are exactly i modulo d. If two characters stand on the positions with the same remainder of integer division by d, their relative order after the sorting shouldn't be changed. The string is zero-indexed. For example, for string 'qwerty':
Its 1-sorting is the string 'qwerty' (all characters stand on 0 positions),
Its 2-sorting is the string 'qetwry' (characters 'q', 'e' and 't' stand on 0 positions and characters 'w', 'r' and 'y' are on 1 positions),
Its 3-sorting is the string 'qrwtey' (characters 'q' and 'r' stand on 0 positions, characters 'w' and 't' stand on 1 positions and characters 'e' and 'y' stand on 2 positions),
Its 4-sorting is the string 'qtwyer',
Its 5-sorting is the string 'qywert'.

You are given string S of length n and m shuffling operations of this string. Each shuffling operation accepts two integer arguments k and d and transforms string S as follows. For each i from 0 to n - k in the increasing order we apply the operation of d-sorting to the substring S[i..i + k - 1]. Here S[a..b] represents a substring that consists of characters on positions from a to b inclusive.
After each shuffling operation you need to print string S.
input: The first line of the input contains a non-empty string S of length n, consisting of lowercase and uppercase English letters and digits from 0 to 9.
The second line of the input contains integer m – the number of shuffling operations (1 ≤ m·n ≤ 106).
Following m lines contain the descriptions of the operations consisting of two integers k and d (1 ≤ d ≤ k ≤ n).
output: After each operation print the current state of string S.
note: Here is detailed explanation of the sample. The first modification is executed with arguments k = 4, d = 2. That means that you need to apply 2-sorting for each substring of length 4 one by one moving from the left to the right. The string will transform in the following manner:
qwerty  →  qewrty  →  qerwty  →  qertwy
Thus, string S equals 'qertwy' at the end of first query.
The second modification is executed with arguments k = 6, d = 3. As a result of this operation the whole string S is replaced by its 3-sorting:
qertwy  →  qtewry
The third modification is executed with arguments k = 5, d = 2.
qtewry  →  qertwy  →  qetyrw

legend: Khaled is the CEO of a rapidly growing industrial empire. His company recently acquired $$$N$$$ new factories, and he has hired $$$N$$$ workers to operate them. Both the workers' homes and the factories are located along a long, straight highway, which can be represented as the $$$X$$$-axis.

The $$$i$$$-th worker lives at coordinate $$$x_i$$$, and the $$$j$$$-th factory is located at coordinate $$$y_j$$$. Khaled needs to assign exactly one worker to each factory so that no two workers are assigned to the same factory.

Khaled requires a "stable" assignment. An assignment is invalid if swapping two workers' factories strictly increases the sum of their squared travel distances. Formally, for any worker $$$i$$$ assigned to factory $$$a$$$ and worker $$$j$$$ assigned to factory $$$b$$$, the following condition must NOT hold:
Given the locations, help Khaled find any valid assignment satisfying his strict stability condition.
input: The first line contains a single integer $$$t$$$ ($$$1 \le t \le 10^4$$$) — the number of test cases.
The first line of each test case contains a single integer $$$N$$$ ($$$1 \le N \le 3000$$$) — the number of workers and the number of factories.
The second line of each test case contains $$$N$$$ distinct integers $$$x_1, x_2, \dots, x_N$$$ ($$$-10^9 \le x_i \le 10^9$$$) — the coordinates of the workers.
The third line of each test case contains $$$N$$$ distinct integers $$$y_1, y_2, \dots, y_N$$$ ($$$-10^9 \le y_i \le 10^9$$$) — the coordinates of the factories.
It is guaranteed that the sum of $$$N$$$ over all test cases does not exceed $$$3000$$$.
output: For each test case, output a single line containing $$$N$$$ space-separated integers $$$p_1, p_2, \dots, p_N$$$, where $$$p_i$$$ is the 1-based index of the factory assigned to the $$$i$$$-th worker.
If there are multiple valid assignments that satisfy Khaled's condition, you may output any of them.

statement.title: D. Where were you 14 years ago?

legend: This is an interactive problem.
After the war in T-Land ended, the people were divided into three groups:
The fighters who liberated the country, called Thowwar, denoted by the letter T.
The supporters of the previous regime despite all of its crimes, called Floul, denoted by the letter F.
People with no opinion or clear identity, called Mkaw3, denoted by the letter M.
There are $$$n$$$ people in the waiting room. Your task is to determine the type of every person.
Fortunately, you can ask Abu Dujana for help. He is able to identify people's apparent identities by simply looking at them.
You may perform the following operation any number of times:
Choose exactly $$$k$$$ ($$$2 \le k \le n$$$) people and send them into Abu Dujana's inspection room.
Their behavior is as follows:   Every Thowwar remains a Thowwar.
Every Floul remains a Floul.
If a Mkaw3 does not find any Thowwar inside the room, they feel safe and return to their original nature as a Floul.
Otherwise, if there is at least one Thowwar in the room, every Mkaw3 immediately starts singing "Labat Labat" and successfully fools Abu Dujana into thinking they are a Thowwar.
Formally, let the chosen group contain $$$T$$$ Thowwar, $$$F$$$ Floul, and $$$M$$$ Mkaw3. Abu Dujana returns a single integer:
If $$$T = 0$$$, Abu Dujana returns $$$0$$$.
Otherwise, Abu Dujana returns $$$T + M$$$.
Determine the type of every person while using at most 812 operations (in honor of 8/12, T-Land Liberation Day).
It is guaranteed that among the $$$n$$$ people there is at least one Thowwar, at least one Floul and at least one Mkaw3.
input: The first line contains a single integer $$$n$$$ ($$$3 \le n \le 400$$$) — the number of people.
The first line of the input contains a single integer $$$n$$$ ($$$3 \le n \le 400$$$) — the number of people.
To ask a query, print a line in the following format:
where $$$2 \le k \le n$$$, all indices are distinct, and $$$1 \le i_j \le n$$$.
After printing a query, flush the output and read a single integer $$$x$$$.
Suppose the chosen group contains:
$$$T$$$ Thowwar,
$$$F$$$ Floul,
$$$M$$$ Mkaw3een.
The interactor responds as follows:
If $$$T = 0$$$, it returns $$$0$$$.
Otherwise, it returns $$$T + M$$$.
You may ask at most 812 queries.
When you have determined the type of every person, print
where $$$s$$$ is a string of length $$$n$$$, and the $$$i$$$-th character is:
T if the $$$i$$$-th person is a Thowwar;
F if the $$$i$$$-th person is a Floul;
M if the $$$i$$$-th person is a Mkaw3.
After printing the answer, terminate your program immediately.
Your program will receive the verdict Wrong Answer if it asks more than $$$812$$$ queries or prints an invalid query.
Remember to flush the output after every query. For example, use:
fflush(stdout) in C/C++;
System.out.flush() in Java;
stdout.flush() in Python;
flush(output) in Pascal.
note: In the sample, there are $$$n = 5$$$ people. The hidden identities are FMTMF (Persons $$$1$$$ and $$$5$$$ are Floul, Persons $$$2$$$ and $$$4$$$ are Mkaw3, and Person $$$3$$$ is Thowwar).
The interaction proceeds as follows:

Query 1 (? 5 1 2 3 4 5): You send everyone to the room. The group contains $$$1$$$ Thowwar (Person $$$3$$$), $$$2$$$ Floul (Persons $$$1$$$ and $$$5$$$), and $$$2$$$ Mkaw3 (Persons $$$2$$$ and $$$4$$$). Because there is at least one Thowwar present ($$$T = 1$$$), the Mkaw3 people act like Thowwar. Abu Dujana returns $$$T + M = 1 + 2 = 3$$$.

Query 2 (? 3 1 2 5): You send persons $$$1$$$, $$$2$$$, and $$$5$$$ to the room. The group contains $$$2$$$ Floul and $$$1$$$ Mkaw3. Since there are absolutely no Thowwar present ($$$T = 0$$$), the Mkaw3 person feels safe and acts like a Floul. Abu Dujana returns $$$0$$$.
Query 3 (? 2 1 5): You send persons $$$1$$$ and $$$5$$$. Both are Floul ($$$T = 0$$$). Abu Dujana returns $$$0$$$.
Query 4 (? 2 3 5): You send persons $$$3$$$ and $$$5$$$. The group contains $$$1$$$ Thowwar and $$$1$$$ Floul. There are no Mkaw3 ($$$M = 0$$$). Abu Dujana returns $$$T + M = 1 + 0 = 1$$$.
Final Answer (! FMTMF): Having deduced the correct types, you print the final string.

problems.hint: You need at least $n$ operations. And luckily, that is achievable.

legend: There is an $$$n$$$ by $$$n$$$ grid of white squares, each containing a bidirectional horizontal or vertical arrow. In one operation, you can choose any square, and based on the arrow in that square, color all squares in the corresponding row or column black. For example, here is one possible sequence of two operations on a grid with $$$n=4$$$:
![](https://espresso.codeforces.com/aeab87caa7ce60dda422a2da0ea4774f1de52b19.png)
What is the minimum number of operations needed to color all squares black, and which squares should you choose in the operations?
input: The first line of the input contains a single integer $$$t$$$ ($$$1\le t\le 250$$$) — the number of test cases.
The first line of each test case contains a single integer $$$n$$$ ($$$1\le n \le 1000$$$) — the number of rows and columns in the grid.

The $$$i$$$-th of the next $$$n$$$ lines contains $$$n$$$ characters each. The $$$j$$$-th of these is $$$\texttt{H}$$$ if the square in position $$$(i, j)$$$ contains a horizontal arrow, and $$$\texttt{V}$$$ if it contains a vertical arrow.
It is guaranteed that the sum of $$$n$$$ over all test cases does not exceed $$$1000$$$.
output: The first line of output for each test case should contain a single integer $$$k$$$ ($$$0 \le k \le n^2$$$) — the number of operations you will perform.
Each of the next $$$k$$$ lines should contain two integers $$$i$$$ and $$$j$$$ ($$$1 \le i, j \le n$$$) — the row and column of the square you will choose for that operation, respectively.
If there are multiple solutions with minimal $$$k$$$, you can print any.
note: The first test case corresponds to the picture above. It can be shown that it is impossible to color everything black in less than $$$4$$$ operations.
In the second test case, since there is only one square, doing a single operation and choosing that square is sufficient to color everything black.

problems.hint: Find the smallest set that is not achievable from vertex $1$ .

legend: You are given a directed graph. For each vertex $$$v$$$, you can remove up to half of the edges directed away from $$$v$$$. Formally, if there are $$$x$$$ edges directed away from $$$v$$$, you can remove up to $$$\lfloor \frac{x}{2} \rfloor$$$ of them. Remove edges in such a way that vertex $$$n$$$ is not reachable from vertex $$$1$$$ or state that this is impossible.
For example, in the below graph, one solution is to remove the three red edges. Note that no vertex has more than half of the edges directed away from it colored red.
![](https://espresso.codeforces.com/438a4e761d9b8095ed1c46dea1ac8210551618ae.png)
input: The first line of the input contains a single integer $$$t$$$ ($$$1\le t\le 10^4$$$) — the number of test cases.
The first line of each test case contains two integers $$$n$$$ and $$$m$$$ ($$$1\le n \le 2\cdot 10^5, 0 \le m \le 2\cdot 10^5$$$) — the number of vertices and edges in the graph, respectively.

Each of the next $$$m$$$ lines contains two integers $$$u$$$ and $$$v$$$ ($$$1 \le u, v \le n, u \ne v$$$), indicating that there is a directed edge from $$$u$$$ to $$$v$$$. All $$$(u, v)$$$ pairs are guaranteed to be distinct, but it is possible for there to be both an edge $$$(u, v)$$$ and an edge $$$(v, u)$$$.
It is guaranteed that both the sum of $$$n$$$ and the sum of $$$m$$$ over all test cases do not exceed $$$2\cdot 10^5$$$.
output: For each test case, if there is no solution, print $$$-1$$$.
Otherwise, the first line of output should contain a single integer $$$k$$$ ($$$0 \le k \le m$$$) — the number of edges to remove.

Each of the next $$$k$$$ lines should contain two integers $$$u$$$ and $$$v$$$ ($$$1 \le u, v \le n$$$) — one of the edges $$$(u, v)$$$ that should be removed. $$$(u, v)$$$ must be present in the input graph, and no edge can be removed twice. Vertex $$$n$$$ should not be reachable from vertex $$$1$$$ after these removals.
If there are multiple solutions, print any.
note: The first test case corresponds to the image above. There are other solutions, such as choosing to only remove the edges $$$(1, 5)$$$ and $$$(4, 2)$$$.
In the second test case, the only valid solution is to remove only the edge $$$(2, 4)$$$.
![](https://espresso.codeforces.com/ccf03c636df8cf95424345d20600b11160a18e6a.png)
This is the graph for the third test case. It can be shown there is no solution.
![](https://espresso.codeforces.com/bc761ec6385bf4d49210e72606698e3b871b5e47.png)

legend: You have a set $$$S$$$ containing the first $$$n$$$ powers of $$$2$$$. However, Thomas tampered with your set and negated some of its values. For example, for $$$n=4$$$, $$$S = \{1, 2, 4, 8\}$$$, and Thomas could negate the $$$2$$$ and $$$4$$$ to turn $$$S$$$ into $$$\{1, -2, -4, 8\}$$$.
You are given a positive integer $$$k$$$. Express $$$k$$$ as the sum of some subset of $$$S$$$, or state that this is impossible.
input: The first line of the input contains a single integer $$$t$$$ ($$$1\le t\le 10^4$$$) — the number of test cases.
The first line of each test case contains two integers $$$n$$$ and $$$k$$$ ($$$1\le n \le 30$$$, $$$1 \le k  \lt  2^n$$$) — the size of $$$S$$$ and the target sum, respectively.
The next line consists of $$$n$$$ characters $$$+$$$ and $$$-$$$, where the $$$i$$$-th character is $$$-$$$ if Thomas negated $$$2^{i-1}$$$ and $$$+$$$ otherwise.
output: For each test case, if there is no subset adding up to $$$k$$$, print $$$-1$$$.

Otherwise, print a string of $$$n$$$ characters $$$\texttt{#}$$$ and $$$\texttt{.}$$$, where the $$$i$$$-th character is $$$\texttt{#}$$$ if you include the $$$i$$$-th element in the subset, and $$$\texttt{.}$$$ otherwise.
If there are multiple solutions, you can print any.
note: In the first test case, $$$S = \{1, -2, -4, 8\}$$$ and $$$k=2$$$. We can choose the subset $$$\{-2, -4, 8\}$$$, which adds up to $$$2$$$.
In the second test case, $$$S = \{-1, -2, -4\}$$$. Since all elements of $$$S$$$ are negative, we cannot choose a subset of $$$S$$$ that adds up to $$$k=5$$$.

legend: Alice and Bob have been close ever since high school. Now they both study at Martian University (MU), but in different departments located far apart. Their schedules are packed, and their classes take place in buildings scattered across the campus. Even though they want to spend time together, they can only meet during the short breaks between their classes.

The campus has $$$N$$$ buildings connected by $$$M$$$ undirected roads. Each road requires a certain amount of time to walk. Both Alice and Bob have several classes throughout the day, each class occurs at a specific building and lasts between a given start and end time. Class intervals do not overlap for each student. Since days on Mars do not follow Earth's fixed length, MU measures time on its own continuous scale, and a single day may be arbitrarily long. As a result, class start and end times can be large values.

Between two consecutive classes of their own, a student may roam the campus freely, traveling along any roads and visiting any buildings, as long as they arrive at their next class on time. Alice and Bob can meet only if they are in the same building at the same moment, during free periods for both. They are dedicated to their studies and will not be late to any class. They also work part time before and after their class schedules, so they will only meet between classes, never before the first class or after the last one.
Alice and Bob may choose different buildings to meet during different free intervals. Your task is to determine the maximum total time they can spend together during the day.
input: The first line contains one integer $$$t$$$ $$$(1 \le t \le 10)$$$, the number of test cases.

Each test case begins with a line containing two integers $$$N$$$ and $$$M$$$ $$$(1 \le N \le 200,\ 1 \le M \le \frac{N(N-1)}{2})$$$, where $$$N$$$ is the number of buildings and $$$M$$$ is the number of roads. Each of the next $$$M$$$ lines contains three integers $$$u, v, w$$$ $$$(1 \le u, v \le N,\ 1 \le w \le 10^5)$$$, describing a bidirectional road between buildings $$$u$$$ and $$$v$$$ with travel time $$$w$$$ minutes.

Then a line follows containing two integers $$$A$$$ and $$$B$$$, the number of classes Alice and Bob have, respectively. The next $$$A$$$ lines describe Alice's classes; each line contains three integers $$$start, end, loc$$$ $$$(1 \le start  \lt  end \le 10^{15},\ 1 \le loc \le N)$$$. After that, the next $$$B$$$ lines describe Bob's classes in the same format.
The sum of $$$A + B$$$ over all test cases does not exceed $$$2 \cdot 10^5$$$.
output: For each test case, print a single integer — the maximum total time Alice and Bob can spend together.

legend: Recently Manya learned that a permutation is a sequence of $$$n$$$ distinct integers from $$$1$$$ to $$$n$$$ in arbitrary order. For example, $$$2,3,1,5,4$$$ is a permutation, but $$$1,2,2$$$ is not a permutation ($$$2$$$ appears twice) and $$$1,3,4$$$ is also not a permutation ($$$n=3$$$ but there is $$$4$$$ in the sequence).

Manya started to write down random permutations, one under another. She wrote down $$$n-1$$$ permutations and realized that a column in the resulting table of integers can also turn out to be a permutation when Manya writes down the $$$n$$$th permutation. Every column will consist of $$$n$$$ integers from $$$1$$$ to $$$n$$$, however, not every column will be a valid permutation. Then Many decided to add the $$$n$$$th permutation in a way to maximize the number of columns-permutations.

Your task is to find out the maximum number of columns that could be permutations after adding the $$$n$$$th permutation; and how many permutations will result in the highest number of columns-permutations.
input: The first line contains a single integer $$$n$$$ — the permutation length ($$$2 \le n \le 1000$$$).
Each of the next $$$n-1$$$ lines contains a permutation of length $$$n$$$ — $$$n$$$ integers from $$$1$$$ to $$$n$$$.
output: Output two integers — the maximum number of column-permutations that can be achieved after adding a permutation; and the number of permutations that can be added to achieve the highest number of columns-permutations modulo $$$10^9 + 7$$$.
note: In the first example, the first column needs $$$2$$$ to be a permutation as well as the fourth column, the third column needs $$$1$$$. Manya can add permutations:
to get two columns-permutations. It is not possible to get a result with three columns-permutations as the $$$n$$$th permutation can not contain two $$$2$$$.

In the second example, none of the columns will be a valid permutation, no matter what permutation Manya adds. That means that the maximum number of columns-permutations is $$$0$$$ and can be achieved by adding any of the $$$24$$$ permutations.

legend: Alexandrik — a well-known security software developer. Today he thought he'd been hacked, so he decided to update the passwords on all his accounts.

To do that, Alexandrik invented a special hard-to-crack string $$$s$$$, which for some reason consists only of the letters a' and b'. And now he wants to choose the largest «perfectly protected» substring from it, for only it will ensure the safety of his precious personal data. Recall that a substring is a contiguous subsegment of a string. For example, for string ababaaa, string bab is a substring because it lies in that string continuously (ababaaa). At the same time, the string abb is not a substring, because although it enters this string (ababaaa), it does not lie in this string continuously. The string bbb is also not a substring, because it does not lie in this string at all.

A string is called «perfectly protected» if it turns out that every character of this string is different from the corresponding character in its «inverted» version (i.e. a string in which the characters of the original string are written in reverse order). So, for example, the string abaabbab is «perfectly protected» because:
abaabbab
babbaabaaba

are distinct in each character. At the same time, the string aaabaabb is not «perfectly protected», because its «inverted» version (babaabaaa) matches the original string in the third and sixth positions.
So, help Alexandrik find the longest substring of his string, which is «perfectly protected».
input: The first line of input contains a single integer $$$n$$$ —the number of characters in the string $$$s$$$ ($$$2 \le n \le 5 \cdot 10^5$$$).
The second line of input data contains the string $$$s$$$ itself, consisting of the letters a' and b'.
output: Print a single non-negative integer — the size of the longest substring of string $$$s$$$, which is «perfectly protected».

legend: Interrail passes are the fun and cheap way to see more of Europe, especially if you combine your train trip with Businesslike And Penny-saving Computation! In particular, you would like to find the cheapest way to pay for your planned travels. You plan to take the train on $$$n$$$ travel days, that are not necessarily consecutive. The individual fare is different for every day, and perhaps you can save money by buying some interrail passes.

There are $$$k$$$ different types of interrail passes with varying costs. Each type of interrail pass can be obtained multiple times. An interrail pass is active for a period of $$$p$$$ consecutive days, that starts on a day of your choice. The interrail pass covers the first $$$d$$$ travel days during this period, which do not have to be consecutive. Note that an active interrail pass cannot be "paused": a day of travel counts towards the day count of each active pass, even when you pay the individual fare that day.

As an example, consider the fourth sample input, visualized in the picture below. It is definitely cheaper to buy interrail passes than to pay $$$4$$$ individual fares. The cheapest solution is to buy two interrail passes of the first type, rather than one interrail pass of the second type.
![](https://espresso.codeforces.com/13d89bb7b2378fe5c7869d05818dc6c0dbed8f8b.png)
input: The input consists of:
One line with two integers $$$n$$$ and $$$k$$$ ($$$1\leq n\leq 10\,000$$$, $$$0\leq k\leq 100$$$), the number of planned travel days, and the number of types of interrail passes available.

$$$n$$$ lines, each with two integers $$$t$$$ and $$$f$$$ ($$$0\leq t \leq 10^6$$$, $$$1\leq f\leq 10^5$$$), the travel day and the individual fare for that day. The $$$n$$$ travel days are distinct and given in increasing order.

$$$k$$$ lines, each with three integers $$$p$$$, $$$d$$$, and $$$c$$$ ($$$1\leq p\leq 10^6$$$, $$$1\leq d\leq p$$$, $$$1\leq c\leq 10^5$$$), indicating a type of interrail pass that is valid for a period of $$$p$$$ days, covers the first $$$d$$$ travel days in that period, and costs $$$c$$$.
output: Output the minimum amount you need to spend to cover all your planned travels.

legend: After participating in the MFP (Matchup of Finalists in Ping-pong) in Campinas, Giovana and Julia are tired of playing ping-pong and decide they need to devise a new sport. They want a sport that, besides physical performance, requires mathematical reasoning and strategy. As both are very fond of binary numbers, they thought of the following game, which they named "Bit Tennis", to play against each other:
The game starts with a string $$$S$$$, of size $$$N$$$, that represents a number in binary;
Giovana begins the game and thereafter they alternate turns between Julia and her;

In each round, the current player can add one more digit ("0" or "1") to the end or the beginning of the string: for example, if the string is "110", the player can turn it into "1100", "1101", "0110" or "1110".
If, after $$$K$$$ turns from each player, the number is a multiple of 3, Julia wins. Otherwise, Giovana wins.

Both quickly learned to play optimally and, after playing a few times, they noticed that the game's outcome is always determined before the first move is even made. Curious about this fact, they asked for your help to, given the initial string and number of turns, find out which one of them will win.
input: The first line of the input consists of the integer $$$N$$$ $$$(1 \leq N \leq 10^5)$$$, the size of the string $$$S$$$, and the integer $$$K$$$ $$$(1 \leq K \leq 10^5)$$$, the number of moves each one will make.
The second line contains the string $$$S$$$, which represents the binary number the game starts with, from the most significant bit to the least significant.
output: Print "GIOVANA" or "JULIA", the name of the winner of the game if both play optimally.

legend: The newly opened Hotel Chevalier is accepting tourists. The hotel boasts $$$n$$$ rooms of various size, the $$$i$$$-th room accommodating $$$c_i$$$ people. $$$k$$$ groups would like to rent a room, the $$$j$$$-th group containing $$$p_j$$$ people and offering $$$m_j$$$ dollars for a room. A room is suitable for some group if and only if its capacity doesn't exceed the number of people in the group. Also, two groups cannot rent the same room.

Unfortunately, it may be possible that the hotel is not large enough to accommodate all groups. Help the hotel manager make the maximum possible revenue for the hotel by optimally assigning rooms to the groups.
input: The first line contains two integers $$$n$$$, $$$k$$$ $$$(1 \le n, k \le 150000)$$$ — the number of rooms in the hotel and the number of tourist groups.
The second line contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$c_i$$$ $$$(1 \le c_i \le 100000)$$$ — the room capacities.
The third line contains $$$k$$$ integers $$$p_i$$$ $$$(1 \le p_i \le 100000)$$$ — the number of tourists in each group.
The fourth line contains $$$k$$$ integers $$$m_i$$$ $$$(1 \le m_i \le 100000)$$$ — the amount of money the groups are willing to pay for a room.
output: Output a single number — the maximum possible amount of money the hotel can make after renting rooms to the tourist groups.

legend: For a positive integer $$$d$$$, let $$$[d]=\{1,2,\dots,d\}$$$. You are given three positive integers $$$a,b,c$$$.
Construct a set $$$S\subseteq[a]\times[b]\times[c]$$$ of integer triples satisfying all of the following conditions:
for every $$$(x,y)\in[a]\times[b]$$$, at least one triple $$$(x,y,z)$$$ belongs to $$$S$$$;
for every $$$(x,z)\in[a]\times[c]$$$, at least one triple $$$(x,y,z)$$$ belongs to $$$S$$$;
for every $$$(y,z)\in[b]\times[c]$$$, at least one triple $$$(x,y,z)$$$ belongs to $$$S$$$.
In other words, deleting any one coordinate from the triples in $$$S$$$ must produce every possible pair of the other two coordinates. The size $$$|S|$$$ must be as small as possible.
input: The first line contains an integer $$$T$$$ ($$$1\le T\le 100$$$), the number of test cases.
For each test case, one line contains three integers $$$a,b,c$$$ ($$$1\le a\le 100$$$, $$$1\le b\le 100$$$, $$$1\le c\le 100$$$).
output: For each test case, print several lines:
The first line contains one integer $$$m$$$, the minimum possible value of $$$|S|$$$.
Each of the next $$$m$$$ lines contains three integers $$$x,y,z$$$, describing one triple in $$$S$$$.
The $$$m$$$ triples must be pairwise distinct. Their order does not matter. If several minimum-size sets are valid, output any one of them.
note: The sample output is one possible answer. Other valid minimum-size sets are also accepted.

problems.hint: How can you compare distances of different paths?

legend: You are given an undirected graph with $$$n$$$ vertices numbered from $$$1$$$ to $$$n$$$ and $$$m$$$ edges. Each edge has an integer weight $$$w$$$ satisfying $$$0\le w \lt k$$$. Parallel edges are allowed, while self-loops are not allowed.

Consider a walk that starts at vertex $$$1$$$ and traverses edges with weights $$$w_1,w_2,\dots,w_L$$$ in this order. A walk may visit vertices and edges more than once. If $$$L\ge1$$$, the total weight of the walk is
$$$$$$ w_1\cdot k^{L-1}+w_2\cdot k^{L-2}+\cdots+w_{L-1}\cdot k+w_L $$$$$$
The empty walk has total weight $$$0$$$.
For every vertex $$$v$$$, let $$$\mathrm{dist}(v)$$$ be the minimum total weight among all walks from vertex $$$1$$$ to vertex $$$v$$$. If no such walk exists, $$$\mathrm{dist}(v)$$$ is undefined.
For every vertex $$$v$$$, determine $$$\mathrm{dist}(v)$$$ modulo $$$998\,244\,353$$$.
input: The first line contains an integer $$$T$$$ ($$$1\le T\le10^4$$$), the number of test cases.
For each test case:

The first line contains three integers $$$n$$$, $$$m$$$, and $$$k$$$ ($$$1\le n\le2\times10^5$$$, $$$0\le m\le5\times10^5$$$, $$$1\le k\le10^9$$$), denoting the number of vertices, the number of edges, and the parameter used in the definition of total weight, respectively.

Each of the next $$$m$$$ lines contains three integers $$$u$$$, $$$v$$$, and $$$w$$$ ($$$1\le u,v\le n$$$, $$$u\ne v$$$, $$$0\le w \lt k$$$), denoting an undirected edge between vertices $$$u$$$ and $$$v$$$ with weight $$$w$$$.
It is guaranteed that the sum of $$$n$$$ over all test cases does not exceed $$$2\times10^5$$$, and the sum of $$$m$$$ over all test cases does not exceed $$$5\times10^5$$$.
output: For each test case, print one line containing $$$n$$$ integers. For each $$$1\le i\le n$$$, consider the $$$i$$$-th integer. If $$$\mathrm{dist}(i)$$$ is defined, it must be $$$\mathrm{dist}(i)$$$ modulo $$$998\,244\,353$$$; otherwise, it must be $$$-1$$$.
note: In the sample, the empty walk gives $$$\mathrm{dist}(1)=0$$$. The one-edge walks give $$$\mathrm{dist}(2)=1$$$ and $$$\mathrm{dist}(3)=2$$$.

There are two two-edge walks from vertex $$$1$$$ to vertex $$$4$$$. Their total weights are $$$1\cdot3+0=3$$$ and $$$2\cdot3+0=6$$$, so $$$\mathrm{dist}(4)=3$$$. Vertex $$$5$$$ is unreachable from vertex $$$1$$$.

legend: During a long bus trip through São Paulo, Miguel likes to observe street signs through the window. The route seems endless: the bus crosses long avenues such as Avenida Sapopemba, Avenida Aricanduva, and Avenida Raimundo Pereira de Magalhães, while Miguel tries to distract himself with the names that appear along the way.
![](https://espresso.codeforces.com/dccdadc4fea4a37b25a08567d020766e9b197f1f.png)

At one point during the trip, as he passes through a region of the city, he sees the same sequence of letters $$$s$$$ repeated $$$p$$$ times. Later, after many stops, he sees the sequence $$$t$$$ repeated $$$q$$$ times.

On the way back home, however, the route is different: first appear the signs with $$$t$$$ repeated $$$q$$$ times, and only afterwards the signs with $$$s$$$ repeated $$$p$$$ times. Miguel decides to mentally compare the two huge letter sequences using lexicographic order, but they are too large to be written out completely.
Given a string $$$u$$$ and a non-negative integer $$$k$$$, let $$$u^k$$$ be the string formed by concatenating $$$k$$$ copies of $$$u$$$. In particular, $$$u^0$$$ is the empty string.

Recall that, in lexicographic order, a string $$$a$$$ is smaller than a string $$$b$$$ if, at the first position where they differ, the character of $$$a$$$ is smaller than the character of $$$b$$$. If one of the strings ends before any difference is found, then the shorter string is considered smaller.
Your task is to compare lexicographically the strings $$$s^p t^q$$$ and $$$t^q s^p$$$.
input: The first line of the input contains the strings $$$s$$$ and $$$t$$$.
The second line contains the integers $$$p$$$ and $$$q$$$.
The strings $$$s$$$ and $$$t$$$ are non-empty and consist only of lowercase English letters, satisfying $$$1 \leq |s|, |t| \leq 200\,000$$$.
The integers satisfy $$$0 \leq p, q \leq 10^9$$$.
output: The output must contain a single line with one character: "=", if $$$s^p t^q$$$ and $$$t^q s^p$$$ are equal; "<", if $$$s^p t^q$$$ is lexicographically smaller than $$$t^q s^p$$$; or ">", otherwise.
