legend: This is an interactive problem.

You are given a maze that consists of a grid of N×M%%ZSMJ0%% (3≤N,M≤30%%ZSMJ1%%) rooms. Any two rooms that are adjacent by a side are connected by a bidirectional colored corridor. There are only four colors that the corridors can be painted: red, green, blue, and yellow.

One of the rooms in the maze is the starting room, and one is the ending room. You can only move between adjacent rooms through the connecting corridors. You are allowed to move through a corridor into another room and then return. As you move, a sequence of your moves is formed. When you move forward, the color of the corridor you are passing through is added to the sequence, and when you move back, the last element is removed from the sequence. However, there is one restriction: you cannot pass through a corridor of color C%%ZSMJ2%% if among the last three elements of the sequence there is C%%ZSMJ3%%.

Neither the maze, the starting position, nor the ending position are known to the participant. You need to reach the ending room from the starting room. It is guaranteed that the ending room is reachable.
Interaction

At the beginning, the jury program outputs two numbers N%%ZSMJ4%% and M%%ZSMJ5%%. Then for each move the participant makes, the jury program outputs the success of that step or asks to end the program if the participant has reached the ending room.
Each move must be one of these commands:
"MOVE LEFT" — if you want to go to the room located to the left of you;
"MOVE RIGHT" — if you want to go to the room located to the right of you;
"MOVE UP" — if you want to go to the room located above you;
"MOVE DOWN" — if you want to go to the room located below you;
"BACK" — to move back.
The jury program will reply with one of these:
"OK" — if your move was successful and you moved to another room;
"FAIL" — if your move was unsuccessful, meaning you tried to pass through a corridor of an invalid color or tried to go back with an empty sequence;
"EXIT" — if you have reached the ending room.
Starting from test 22%%ZSMJ6%%, the jury's program is adaptive to the participant's program output.
The total number of moves must not exceed 100000%%ZSMJ7%%.
note: In the first test, the jury has the following maze:
![](https://espresso.codeforces.com/9a3b160d6a02e91b4065cf4ccabbd71b3c259984.png)

Black dots represent rooms. The corridors between rooms are represented by lines. The letter next to the corridor indicates its color ("Y" — yellow, "R" — red, "G" — green, "B" — blue). Initially, the participant is in the room marked with a bold dot. Next to the room that is the final destination for the participant is the letter "X". Neither the maze, nor the starting position, nor the ending position are known to the participant.
The first command is BACK, but since there have been no moves yet, nothing happens. The jury program reports that the move was unsuccessful ("FAIL").
The second command is MOVE DOWN. After this, the sequence of colors of the passed corridors will be: "yellow".
The movement is shown in the picture below.
![](https://espresso.codeforces.com/fc9e7a2d6706c465e0deea4b7bb0cddbbe570af8.png)

The next command is MOVE LEFT. With this command, the participant tries to pass through the yellow corridor, which is already the last in the sequence, so the jury informs that the move was unsuccessful.
The next command is MOVE RIGHT. The sequence of colors now becomes: "yellow, blue". The movement is shown in the picture below.
![](https://espresso.codeforces.com/37c03826e36090105014b1360f6d9a6c940bbbfe.png)

In the next three commands, the participant attempts to pass through corridors of blue or yellow colors, which are already included in the last three elements of the sequence, so the jury reports that those moves are unsuccessful.
The following command is BACK. The sequence of moves is: "yellow".
The next command is BACK again. The sequence of moves is: "" (empty).
The next command is MOVE UP. The sequence of moves will be "blue". Since the participant reached the ending room, the jury asks the participant to end the program.

legend: Let's denote the beauty of a string as follows: consider the lengths of all maximal contiguous blocks consisting of the same letters. Then, the beauty of a string is the sum of the squares of the lengths of all such blocks.

For example, let the string be "aabbbcaaadddd". In this string, the following blocks of identical letters exist: a block of two letters "a", a block of three letters "b", a block of one letter "c", a block of three letters "a", and a block of four letters "d". Thus, the beauty of this string is 22+32+12+32+42=4+9+1+9+16=39%%ZSMJ0%%.

Your task is to determine the maximum beauty of the new string that Monocarp can obtain after exactly one swap of adjacent different letters in his string s%%ZSMJ4%%.

there are at least two different letters in the given string.

In the second example, it is possible to swap the fourth and fifth letters. Then Monocarp will get the string "wwwzw". The beauty of this string is 32+12+12=9+1+1=11%%ZSMJ12%%.

legend: This is a run-twice (communication) problem.

legend: There are n%%ZSMJ0%% valuable artifacts arranged in a row, where the i%%ZSMJ1%%-th artifact has a cost ci%%ZSMJ2%%. Thomas is planning on stealing some of the artifacts. The MEX%%ZSMJ4%% of a set of integers is defined as the smallest non-negative integer which does not occur in the set. For example, the MEX%%ZSMJ5%% of {0,1,2,4}%%ZSMJ6%% is 3%%ZSMJ7%%, and the MEX%%ZSMJ8%% of {1,4,6,8}%%ZSMJ9%% is 0%%ZSMJ10%%.
For example, if Thomas has previously stolen artifacts with costs of {1,2,1,0,6,5}%%ZSMJ11%%, the next artifact he steals must have a cost of at least 3%%ZSMJ12%%.

There is a special artifact initially at position k%%ZSMJ13%% in the row, and your goal is to prevent Thomas from stealing it. To do so, you may swap the positions of any pair of artifacts. Is it possible to stop Thomas from stealing the special artifact, and if so, which swap should you make?

If there are multiple solutions, you may print any.
note: In the first test case, we swap artifacts 3%%ZSMJ29%% and 5%%ZSMJ30%%, so this is what the row of artifacts will look like before and after the swap (with the special artifact in red):
After the swap, Thomas will make the following moves, where S%%ZSMJ32%% is the set of costs of artifacts Thomas has stolen.
For the first artifact, S={}%%ZSMJ33%%, with a MEX%%ZSMJ34%% of 0%%ZSMJ35%%. Since c1=1≥0%%ZSMJ36%%, he steals the first artifact and adds 1%%ZSMJ37%% to S%%ZSMJ38%%.
For the second artifact, S={1}%%ZSMJ39%%, with a MEX%%ZSMJ40%% of 0%%ZSMJ41%%. Since c2=0≥0%%ZSMJ42%%, he steals the second artifact and adds 0%%ZSMJ43%% to S%%ZSMJ44%%.
For the third artifact, S={0,1}%%ZSMJ45%%, with a MEX%%ZSMJ46%% of 2%%ZSMJ47%%. Since c3=2≥2%%ZSMJ48%%, he steals the third artifact and adds 2%%ZSMJ49%% to S%%ZSMJ50%%.
For the fourth artifact, S={0,1,2}%%ZSMJ51%%, with a MEX%%ZSMJ52%% of 3%%ZSMJ53%%. Since c4=2<3%%ZSMJ54%%, he does not steal the fourth artifact.
For the fifth artifact, S={0,1,2}%%ZSMJ55%%, with a MEX%%ZSMJ56%% of 3%%ZSMJ57%%. Since c5=1<3%%ZSMJ58%%, he does not steal the fifth artifact.
Since he doesn't steal the special artifact on position 4%%ZSMJ59%%, we have succeeded.
In the second test case, we swap artifacts 1%%ZSMJ60%% and 4%%ZSMJ61%%, so the artifacts will look like this before and after the swap:

legend: You are given arrays a%%ZSMJ0%%, p%%ZSMJ1%%, and q%%ZSMJ2%% of n%%ZSMJ3%% nonnegative integers each, and a multiset S%%ZSMJ4%% that is initially empty. The MEX%%ZSMJ12%% of a set of integers is defined as the smallest non-negative integer which does not occur in the set. For example, the MEX%%ZSMJ13%% of {0,1,2,4}%%ZSMJ14%% is 3%%ZSMJ15%%, and the MEX%%ZSMJ16%% of {1,4,6,8}%%ZSMJ17%% is 0%%ZSMJ18%%.

So \frac{1}{3}%%ZSMJ53%% of the time, S = \{0\}%%ZSMJ54%%, which has a \operatorname{MEX}%%ZSMJ55%% of 1%%ZSMJ56%%, and otherwise S = \{\}%%ZSMJ57%%, with a \operatorname{MEX}%%ZSMJ58%% of 0%%ZSMJ59%%.

In the second test case, we include a_1 = 0%%ZSMJ64%% in S%%ZSMJ65%% with probability \frac{1}{2}%%ZSMJ66%% and a_2 = 1%%ZSMJ67%% in S%%ZSMJ68%% with probability \frac{1}{2}%%ZSMJ69%%. So there are four possible outcomes for S%%ZSMJ70%%, each with probability \frac{1}{4}%%ZSMJ71%% of occurring:
S = \{\}%%ZSMJ72%% with a \operatorname{MEX}%%ZSMJ73%% of 0%%ZSMJ74%%
S = \{0\}%%ZSMJ75%% with a \operatorname{MEX}%%ZSMJ76%% of 1%%ZSMJ77%%
S = \{1\}%%ZSMJ78%% with a \operatorname{MEX}%%ZSMJ79%% of 0%%ZSMJ80%%

In the third test case, we include a_1 = 0%%ZSMJ88%%, a_2 = 0%%ZSMJ89%%, and a_3 = 0%%ZSMJ90%% in S%%ZSMJ91%% each with independent probability \frac{1}{2}%%ZSMJ92%%. legend: This is an interactive problem.

The colony currently consists of n%%ZSMJ0%% male and n%%ZSMJ1%% female ants, each numbered 1%%ZSMJ2%% through n%%ZSMJ3%%. The scientists want to find a female ant to mate with each male ant. Since ants are polyandrous, one female can mate with multiple males at once.

The AI observes their behaviour and reports one pair of ants which are attracted to each other, or that none exist. The cost of this experiment is x+y%%ZSMJ6%% dollars.

"? xi1i2…ixyj1j2…jy%%ZSMJ7%%" — run the experiment on male ants i1,i2,…,ix%%ZSMJ8%% and female ants j1,j2,…,jy%%ZSMJ9%%. legend: Alice is madly in love with Bob and she hopes to impress him by beating him in yet another chocolate game.
The game begins with two piles of chocolate cookies, one on the left and one on the right. Alice and Bob will take turns.

On each player's turn, they must choose exactly one of the piles, and eat some positive number of cookies from it such that the number of cookies remaining is a positive divisor of the previous pile size. Alice and Bob are supergenius, perfectly rational grandmaster prodigies who always make the optimal move in any game they play. Alice considers a game to be WINNABLE if there is some strategy she can follow so that she is guaranteed to win no matter what Bob does (so long as Alice plays correctly). legend: Upon arriving on Mars, astronaut Mark Watney and his team discovered that the planet was not quite as they had expected. Its terrain was filled with large ravines—gaps in the ground—that made it very difficult for the team to traverse the red planet.

Fortunately, the astronauts brought along a set of ladders of various lengths; these ladders allowed them to cross the ravines when laid out horizontally, as long as their extended length was greater than or equal to the size of the gap.

The team has a schedule indicating one coordinate of interest to visit each day, and for these visits, they choose one ladder from their set to help cross the ravines. After reaching the point of interest, the astronauts must return via the same path they came from (back to the area where they reside), and the used ladder is then discarded due to wear and tear, making it unavailable for future days.

Given this, Mark was tasked with developing a program that, when provided with a map showing regions separated by ravines, the lengths of the ravines, the set of ladders brought by the team, and the cities the team wants to visit each day, maximizes the number of regions of interest visited during the entire mission. Mark, being a great biologist but not much of a programmer, called you for help.

The map of Mars is given as a graph with N%%ZSMJ0%% regions numbered from 1%%ZSMJ1%% to N%%ZSMJ2%% and M%%ZSMJ3%% ravines numbered from 1%%ZSMJ4%% to M%%ZSMJ5%% connecting these regions, where the i%%ZSMJ6%%-th ravine has a length of wi%%ZSMJ7%% meters. It is also a fact that if it were possible to use a ladder of infinite length, one could travel from any region to any other region using only the ravines.

Additionally, the mission will last D%%ZSMJ8%% days, where the region to be visited on the i%%ZSMJ9%%-th day is di%%ZSMJ10%%, and the team has exactly D%%ZSMJ11%% ladders numbered from 1%%ZSMJ12%% to D%%ZSMJ13%%, where the length of the i%%ZSMJ14%%-th ladder is ei%%ZSMJ15%%. Note that a ladder can be used on any day, but only once; and during a day, the chosen ladder can be reused as many times as necessary.
Knowing that the team resides in region 1%%ZSMJ16%%, write a program to help Mark's team with their mission!
input: The first line of the input consists of two numbers N%%ZSMJ17%% and M%%ZSMJ18%% (2≤N≤2⋅105)%%ZSMJ19%% (1≤M≤2⋅105)%%ZSMJ20%%, the number of regions and ravines on Mars, respectively.

The next M%%ZSMJ21%% lines each contain three integers ui%%ZSMJ22%%, vi%%ZSMJ23%%, and wi%%ZSMJ24%%, (1≤ui,vi≤N)%%ZSMJ25%% (1≤wi≤109)%%ZSMJ26%%, indicating the existence of a ravine of length wi%%ZSMJ27%% between regions ui%%ZSMJ28%% and vi%%ZSMJ29%%. It is guaranteed that there is only one ravine connecting any two regions, and no ravine connects a region to itself.
Then, a line with a single integer D%%ZSMJ30%% (1≤D≤N)%%ZSMJ31%% is given, representing the number of days in the mission; followed by two lines with D%%ZSMJ32%% integers each.
The first of these lines contains d1,d2,⋯,dD%%ZSMJ33%% (1≤di≤N)%%ZSMJ34%%, indicating that the i%%ZSMJ35%%-th region to be visited is region number di%%ZSMJ36%%.
The next line contains e1,e2,⋯,eD%%ZSMJ37%% (1≤ei≤109)%%ZSMJ38%%, indicating that the i%%ZSMJ39%%-th ladder is ei%%ZSMJ40%% meters long.
output: Print a single line with the maximum number of regions that Mark and his team can visit.
note: Below is the map for the second example:
![](https://espresso.codeforces.com/3c5d5f91757afb2f5186b4548b9b14917b9ffb0c.png)

We can use one of the ladders of length two to reach node 5%%ZSMJ41%% on the first day; then, we can skip the second day's target and use the ladder of length 11%%ZSMJ42%% to reach node 2%%ZSMJ43%% on the third day (through the path 1 – 5 – 2). Note that there may be more than one way to achieve the optimal answer.

legend: Madoka has already finished writing the municipal stage in Novosibirsk and went home to wait for the results of the closed testing.

At the olympiad, there was exactly one problem — given a permutation of numbers from 1%%ZSMJ0%% to n%%ZSMJ1%%: p1,p2,…,pn%%ZSMJ2%%. It is necessary to find out the minimum number of times one can swap adjacent elements to sort the permutation in ascending order. However, Madoka solved it as follows: k+|1−p1|+|2−p2|+…+|n−pn|2%%ZSMJ3%%.

But since the jury knows who Madoka's father is, in order not to lose their job, they must create tests such that Madoka's solution is correct. Therefore, they became interested in how many permutations of length n%%ZSMJ4%% exist for which Madoka's solution will yield the correct answer to the problem, but since the answer may be too large, output it modulo 109+7%%ZSMJ5%%.
input: Two numbers n,k%%ZSMJ6%% are given in a single line separated by a space (2≤n≤17%%ZSMJ7%%, 0≤k≤50%%ZSMJ8%%).
output: In a single line, print exactly the number — the number of permutations of length n%%ZSMJ9%% modulo 109+7%%ZSMJ10%% for which the minimum number of swaps of neighboring elements for sorting is k+|1−p1|+|2−p2|+…+|n−pn|2%%ZSMJ11%%.
note: In the first example, only the permutation 3,2,1%%ZSMJ12%% is suitable, for it the minimum number of swaps is  — 3%%ZSMJ13%%, and Madoka's answer is — |1−3|+|2−2|+|3−1|2+1=2+1=3%%ZSMJ14%%.

legend: Palao and his friends live in the same condominium indexed from 0%%ZSMJ0%% to m−1%%ZSMJ1%%. The condominium has a circular layout because the architect, Peppy, loves circles. From building i%%ZSMJ2%%, you can go to building (i+1)mod%%ZSMJ3%% or to building (i-1) \bmod m%%ZSMJ4%%.

legend: Tiago was playing the famous Directed Bank game with his friends Leonardo, Gabriel, and Paulo.

As everyone knows, the Directed Bank board has N%%ZSMJ0%% positions and M%%ZSMJ1%% possible moves, with the i%%ZSMJ2%%-th move represented by the tuple (Ui,Vi,Wi)%%ZSMJ3%%; that is, if the player is on position Ui%%ZSMJ4%%, they can move to position Vi%%ZSMJ5%%, adding Wi%%ZSMJ6%% to their balance. It's possible for the balance to become negative during the game.
The game always starts from position number 1, and in a round, the player can make a valid move or wait on the same spot, without losing or gaining anything.

Being an expert Directed Bank player, Tiago soon discovers a bug feature in the game! It's possible to accumulate infinite money! But it's not so clear how this could happen, and Leonardo and Gabriel disagreed with the statement, demanding proof. Tiago said he would demonstrate with an example of infinite moves during the game, which would also take an infinitely long time.
But since the pizza they ordered was almost arriving, there was only enough time for Tiago to play a finite number of rounds, and the problem remained open.
Knowing that you are a great programmer and that you are training for the UFPE Programming Contest, Paulo proposed you a challenge: prove or disprove Tiago!

But since infinity is a very long time, you only need to simulate 10998244353%%ZSMJ7%% rounds to convince the group of friends. That is, given the description of the board, state the largest possible average value per round that can be obtained on this board after 10998244353%%ZSMJ8%% rounds.
input: The first line of input contains two integers 2≤N≤2000%%ZSMJ9%%, 1≤M≤2000%%ZSMJ10%%, representing the number of positions on the board and the number of possible valid moves.
The following M%%ZSMJ11%% lines contain three integers Ui,Vi,Wi%%ZSMJ12%%, with 1≤Ui,Vi≤N%%ZSMJ13%% and −109≤Wi≤109%%ZSMJ14%%, where Ui≠Vi%%ZSMJ15%%. This represents the list of valid moves.
Note that multiple edges between the same pair of positions are allowed.
output: Print a real number, the answer to the problem. Your solution will be considered correct if it has a relative or absolute error less than or equal to 10−6%%ZSMJ16%%.
note: In sample 1, a valid strategy is to go from square 1 to square 2, return to square 1, then go to square 2, and so on (1,2,1,2,1,2,…)%%ZSMJ17%%. After infinite rounds, the average points accumulated per round will be 0.5%%ZSMJ18%%.
In sample 2, a valid strategy is to never leave the first square, thus never losing points in the balance.

legend: Pou, Grisi, and Guilherme were starving, so they decided to have dinner at Subway. While they sat waiting for their meals and playing Brawl Stars, the kitchen exploded out of nowhere, sending food flying everywhere! Pou, being the only one quick on his feet, decided to take advantage of the situation to satisfy his hunger. He closed his game and prepared to attack!

All food items and Pou are located on a two-dimensional plane, where y=0%%ZSMJ0%% represents the ground. At time t=0%%ZSMJ1%%, Pou is at position (0,0)%%ZSMJ2%% and the i%%ZSMJ3%%-th food is at position (xi,yi)%%ZSMJ4%%. Each food falls at a constant vertical speed of 1%%ZSMJ5%% unit per second, while Pou can move left or right at a constant speed of 1%%ZSMJ6%% unit per second.

In other words, if in a time t%%ZSMJ7%% a food item is at (x,y)%%ZSMJ8%%, at time t+1%%ZSMJ9%% it will be at (x,y−1)%%ZSMJ10%%. Simultaneously, if in a time t%%ZSMJ11%% Pou is at (x,0)%%ZSMJ12%%, at time t+1%%ZSMJ13%% he can be at (x,0)%%ZSMJ14%%, (x+1,0)%%ZSMJ15%%, or (x−1,0)%%ZSMJ16%%.

Pou can eat food item i%%ZSMJ17%% if and only if he is at position xi%%ZSMJ18%% at the exact moment the food hits the ground (y=0%%ZSMJ19%%). For hygiene reasons, he will not eat any food that has already touched the ground before his arrival.
![](https://espresso.codeforces.com/faab0d7eb8f7663c7b082595bdec0b0b2fc129ea.png)

Grisi and Guilherme were so stunned by the explosion that they forgot how many food items Pou ate, but they remember the initial positions of all the food items. Knowing that Pou ate the maximum possible amount of food, your mission is to determine that number.
input: The input consists of several lines. The first line contains n%%ZSMJ20%% (1≤n≤2⋅103%%ZSMJ21%%), the number of food items.
The following n%%ZSMJ22%% lines contain two integers x%%ZSMJ23%% and y%%ZSMJ24%% (1≤x,y≤106%%ZSMJ25%%), the i%%ZSMJ26%%-th line represents the initial position of food i%%ZSMJ27%%.
It is guaranteed that no two food items occupy the same initial position, that is: ∀i∀j((i≠j)⟹(xi,yi)≠(xj,yj))%%ZSMJ28%%.
output: The output must contain a single integer: the maximum number of food items Pou could have eaten.

legend: Gab "gabmei" mei is known for his hacks in Codeforces contests. He once hacked three marathonists in the same contest!

Triple kill!

legend: Toni was walking through the wild CIn parking lot, dodging beasts and trying to find where he parked his car when he stumbled upon a formidable object: a stick of exact integer length n%%ZSMJ0%%.

Like any good problem-solver, Toni's mind immediately thought of a "gambiarra" (a makeshift solution). He needs to build a support base for his new hardware project. For the base to be stable, he needs to form a perfect triangle using pieces of this stick.
However, Toni is exhausted after a coding marathon. He decides to cut the stick at two distinct points, chosen completely at random. He only has energy for these two cuts.
Your mission is to calculate the chances of Toni's plan working, so he knows whether or not to give up and go grab a coffee.
![](https://espresso.codeforces.com/2d63752433be2a9f7e9e75e8453102c8488677ec.png)
Formally, we have a line segment of length n%%ZSMJ1%%. The set of possible cut points consists of the internal integer coordinates {1,2,…,n−1}%%ZSMJ2%%.

Toni chooses two distinct cut points from this set, uniformly at random. This divides the original stick into three pieces with positive integer lengths a%%ZSMJ3%%, b%%ZSMJ4%%, and c%%ZSMJ5%% (such that a+b+c=n%%ZSMJ6%%).
What is the probability that these three resulting pieces (a,b,c%%ZSMJ7%%) can form a non-degenerate triangle (i.e., a triangle with an area greater than zero)?
Since the answer can be an irreducible fraction pq%%ZSMJ8%%, you must print the value of p⋅q−1(mod109+7)%%ZSMJ9%%, where q−1%%ZSMJ10%% is the modular inverse of q%%ZSMJ11%% modulo 109+7%%ZSMJ12%%.
input: The first line of the input contains a single integer t%%ZSMJ13%% (1≤t≤105%%ZSMJ14%%) — the number of test cases. Each of the following t%%ZSMJ15%% lines contains a single integer n%%ZSMJ16%% (3≤n≤109%%ZSMJ17%%), representing the length of the stick Toni found in that specific scenario.
output: For each test case, print a single integer on a new line: the probability of the makeshift solution working, modulo 109+7%%ZSMJ18%%.

Players take turns, and on each turn, the current player must choose a non-empty subset of the remaining numbers and remove it. Whenever a subset of X%%ZSMJ2%% numbers is removed, the remaining numbers are relabeled to be the smallest consecutive values starting from 2. That is, if there were Y%%ZSMJ3%% numbers before the move, the numbers after the removal become 2,3,4,…,Y+1−X%%ZSMJ4%%.

legend: Your guests are not committed to a standardised order of sandwich assembly, and that makes it difficult to know which order to place each of the n%%ZSMJ0%% ingredients in on the sandwich bar. You have lots of other food related things to do, so you decide to just place the ingredients down according to your own preference, at arbitrary distinct locations on your table top. Now your guests will have to travel back and forth along the table placing ingredients in their preferred order.

Supposing that order preferences are indeed uniformly random amongst your guests (that is, each permutation of ingredients is equally likely to be the preference), and given the positions of each of the locations of the ingredients in the order you like in meters, what is the expected time a guest takes to assemble a sandwich? Each guest travels at one meter per second. Answer in seconds.

Each guest begins at the leftmost end of the table, at position 0%%ZSMJ1%%, and exits the sandwich bar at the rightmost end, position W%%ZSMJ2%%, where W%%ZSMJ3%% is the width of the table. Each guest takes every ingredient in exactly the order they prefer.

Every guest travels at 1%%ZSMJ13%% meter per second.
output: Output a single number that is the expected time in seconds for a random guest to collect the ingredients of their sandwich in the order they desire.

statement.title: I. Riana and the Illuminous Triangles

legend: Riana always wanted to join the secret order of the ProgVar. Most people doubt its existence, believing it to be just a myth propagated by paranoid conspiracy theorists. However, some, including Riana, know the truth: ProgVar is an immensely influential organization working behind the scenes to control the world at large.

The all-knowing ProgVar, of course, is aware of her intent. One day, she received an initiation parchment. The parchment contains a geometric graph of n%%ZSMJ0%% points, no three of which are collinear. Riana knows that ProgVar is obsessed with triangles, and that she may form a triangle from any three of the n%%ZSMJ1%% points.

To demonstrate her commitment to joining the order, she must count how many ways there are of forming two triangles such that one triangle lies entirely within the other. In particular, these two triangles must not share a vertex. Two ways of forming triangles are considered distinct if there is a point that is used as a triangle vertex in one way but not in the other way.

Riana, of course, is a capable follower, and she sent her answers to the order in less than two seconds. ProgVar, busy with more important world affairs, has outsourced the task of checking her answers to you. How many such ways of forming two triangles are there?
input: The first line contains the number of points n≤300%%ZSMJ2%%.
The next n%%ZSMJ3%% lines each contains two integers x%%ZSMJ4%% and y%%ZSMJ5%%, where the i%%ZSMJ6%%th line denotes that the i%%ZSMJ7%%th point is (x,y)%%ZSMJ8%%.
The absolute values of the coordinates of each point are guaranteed not to exceed 104%%ZSMJ9%%.
output: Print how many such ways there are of forming two triangles that satisfy the problem.
Note that the answer may exceed 1010%%ZSMJ10%%.
note: ![](https://espresso.codeforces.com/4aaa73fbe4873533515b446ff48cab0253ebd499.png)
It may also be shown that there are no other pairs of triangles that satisfy the problem conditions. Therefore, the answer for the first test case is 4%%ZSMJ11%%.

problems.hint: What is the maximum number of operations needed? Then it's about finding different cases.

legend: You are given a string S%%ZSMJ0%% of length 3n%%ZSMJ1%%, consisting of the characters A, B and C. You are allowed to perform the following operation:
Select some subsegment of this string and a character c%%ZSMJ2%% (one of A, B and C). Then, replace all the characters on the subsegment with c%%ZSMJ3%%.

Find the smallest number of times that you would have to apply the operation above to get a string which contains each of characters A, B and C exactly n%%ZSMJ4%% times. It can be shown that it is always possible to get such a string.
In addition, find a sequence of operations of the smallest possible length. If there are many such sequences, you can output any of them.
input: The first line of input contains a single integer n%%ZSMJ5%% (1≤n≤3⋅105%%ZSMJ6%%).
The second line of the input contains a string S%%ZSMJ7%% of length 3n%%ZSMJ8%%, consisting of the characters A, B and C.
output: In the first line print the minimum number of operations k%%ZSMJ9%%.

In the i%%ZSMJ10%%-th of the next k%%ZSMJ11%% lines print 2%%ZSMJ12%% integers li,ri%%ZSMJ13%% and a character ci%%ZSMJ14%% (1≤li≤ri≤3n%%ZSMJ15%%, ci∈{A,B,C}%%ZSMJ16%%), denoting that in the i%%ZSMJ17%%-th operation you will replace each of the characters Sli,Sli+1,…,Sri%%ZSMJ18%% with ci%%ZSMJ19%%.
If there is more than one solution with a minimum number of operations, you can print any one of them.
note: In the first sample, the string will undergo the following transformations:
AAA →%%ZSMJ20%% ABB →%%ZSMJ21%% ABC.
In the second sample, the string already contains exactly one A, one B and one C.
In the third sample, the string will undergo the following transformation:
ABABCABAB →%%ZSMJ22%% CCABCABAB. Now, it contains each letter 3%%ZSMJ23%% times.

legend: The scientists invented the new UL-2018 processor that is able to quickly process arrays in some special way. A key feature of its architecture is the separation operation of a segment of the array.

Consider an array [a1,a2,…,an]%%ZSMJ0%%. The separation operation is characterized by two integers L%%ZSMJ1%% and R%%ZSMJ2%%. Let S(L,R)%%ZSMJ3%% denote the operation of the segment [aL,aL+1,…,aR]%%ZSMJ4%%. Executing the S(L,R)%%ZSMJ5%% operation reorders the elements in this segment as follows. First, the elements aL+1,aL+3,aL+5,…%%ZSMJ6%% are taken, that is elements ai%%ZSMJ7%% that i−L%%ZSMJ8%% is odd. Their relative order remains unchanged. Then, the elements aL,aL+2,aL+4,…%%ZSMJ9%% are taken (ai%%ZSMJ10%% that i−L%%ZSMJ11%% is even). These retain the relative order too.

For example, consider the array [2,4,1,5,3,6,7,8]%%ZSMJ12%%. Applying the operation S(2,6)%%ZSMJ13%% changes the segment [4,1,5,3,6]%%ZSMJ14%% into [1,3,4,5,6]%%ZSMJ15%%, so the entire array becomes [2,1,3,4,5,6,7,8]%%ZSMJ16%%.

To demonstrate the capabilities of the new processor, the scientists decided to use separation operations to sort an array of distinct numbers. You will be given an array of size n%%ZSMJ17%% (1≤n≤3000%%ZSMJ18%%) with distinct numbers from 1%%ZSMJ19%% to n%%ZSMJ20%%. You must sort it in ascending order using no more than 15000%%ZSMJ21%% separation operations.

For example, the mentioned array [2,4,1,5,3,6,7,8]%%ZSMJ22%% can be sorted in two separation operations. First, apply S(2,6)%%ZSMJ23%% to get [2,1,3,4,5,6,7,8]%%ZSMJ24%%, and then the operation S(1,2)%%ZSMJ25%% makes the array sorted increasingly: [1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8]%%ZSMJ26%%.

Your task is to write a program that for a given array determines the sequence of at most 15000%%ZSMJ27%% separation operations, after which the specified array will be sorted in ascending order. It isn't necessary to minimize the number of operations performed (just use at most 15000%%ZSMJ28%%).
input: The first line of the input contains an integer n%%ZSMJ29%% — the number of elements in the given array (1≤n≤3000%%ZSMJ30%%).
The second line contains n%%ZSMJ31%% distinct integers a1,a2,…,an%%ZSMJ32%% — the elements of the given array (1≤ai≤n%%ZSMJ33%%, all ai%%ZSMJ34%% are different).
output: The first line of the output should contain an integer k%%ZSMJ35%% — the number of separation operations performed (0≤k≤15000%%ZSMJ36%%).

In the following k%%ZSMJ37%% lines, you should print the description of the operations, in the order they are executed. Each operation is described by two integers L%%ZSMJ38%% and R%%ZSMJ39%% — the beginning and the end of the segment to which the separation operation should be applied (1≤L≤R≤n%%ZSMJ40%%).

Note that you don't have to minimize the number k%%ZSMJ41%%. You can output any sequence of separation operations that contains at most 15000%%ZSMJ42%% operations and sorts the given array in ascending order. It is guaranteed that at least one such sequence exists.
SubtaskPointsConstraintsDependencies120n≤100; there is a solution with k=1230n≤1000,1330n≤10000−2420n≤30000−3%%ZSMJ43%%
You will get points for a group if you pass all tests in this group and all groups listed in the dependencies. The group 0%%ZSMJ44%% denotes the sample test(s) from the statement.
note: The second sample test is analyzed in detail in the problem statement.
In the third sample test, there is a solution with a single separation operation, but since you don't have to minimize the number of operations, the provided output is also correct.

legend: Leo Jr. draws pictures in his notebook with checkered sheets (that is, each sheet has a regular square grid printed on it). We can assume that the sheets are infinitely large in any direction.
To draw a picture, Leo Jr. colors some of the cells on a sheet gray. He considers the resulting picture beautiful if the following conditions are satisfied:

The picture is connected, that is, it is possible to get from any gray cell to any other by following a chain of gray cells, with each pair of adjacent cells in the path being neighbours (that is, sharing a side).
Each gray cell has an even number of gray neighbours.
There are exactly n%%ZSMJ0%% gray cells with all gray neighbours. The number of other gray cells can be arbitrary (but reasonable, so that they can all be listed).
Leo Jr. is now struggling to draw a beautiful picture with a particular choice of n%%ZSMJ1%%. Help him, and provide any example of a beautiful picture.

To output cell coordinates in your answer, assume that the sheet is provided with a Cartesian coordinate system such that one of the cells is chosen to be the origin (0,0)%%ZSMJ2%%, axes 0x%%ZSMJ3%% and 0y%%ZSMJ4%% are orthogonal and parallel to grid lines, and a unit step along any axis in any direction takes you to a neighbouring cell.
input: The only line contains a single integer n%%ZSMJ5%% (1≤n≤500%%ZSMJ6%%) — the number of gray cells with all gray neighbours in a beautiful picture.
output: In the first line, print a single integer k%%ZSMJ7%% — the number of gray cells in your picture. For technical reasons, k%%ZSMJ8%% should not exceed 5⋅105%%ZSMJ9%%.

Each of the following k%%ZSMJ10%% lines should contain two integers — coordinates of a gray cell in your picture. All listed cells should be distinct, and the picture should satisdfy all the properties listed above. All coordinates should not exceed 109%%ZSMJ11%% by absolute value.
One can show that there exists an answer satisfying all requirements with a small enough k%%ZSMJ12%%.

Determine the maximum weight of the matching in this graph.

legend: You are given an undirected graph with N%%ZSMJ0%% nodes and a list of edges of size M%%ZSMJ1%%. problems.hint: What's the DP transition? And how can you do it $K$ times efficiently?

legend: After working for over a year in a corporation, Peter realised that this is not the way to get rich. Instead, he quit his job and decided to participate in a lottery.

The lottery consists of a bag of N%%ZSMJ0%% prizes. The value of the ith%%ZSMJ1%% prize is value[i]%%ZSMJ2%% and its weight is weight[i]%%ZSMJ3%%. A prize is chosen randomly from the bag according to its weight. That is, the probability of the ith%%ZSMJ4%% prize to be chosen is weight[i]∑Nk=1weight[k]%%ZSMJ5%%. Now, Peter has a choice to make. He can accept the prize and go home with it, or he can refuse the prize. If Peter refuses, the prize is placed back in the bag and Peter plays another round. However, Peter can refuse at most K%%ZSMJ6%% times. If he refuses K%%ZSMJ7%% times, then he is forced to take home the prize from the K+1th%%ZSMJ8%% round.
Help Peter get rich and compute for him the maximum expected value he can get if he plays optimally.
input: The first line of the input contains the integers N%%ZSMJ9%% (1≤N≤105%%ZSMJ10%%) and K%%ZSMJ11%% (0≤K≤107%%ZSMJ12%%), denoting the number of prizes in the bag and the maximum number of times Peter can refuse the prize.

Each of the following N%%ZSMJ13%% lines contains 2%%ZSMJ14%% integers value[i]%%ZSMJ15%% and weight[i]%%ZSMJ16%% (1≤value[i],weight[i]≤105%%ZSMJ17%%), denoting the value and the weight of the ith%%ZSMJ18%% prize.
output: On a single line, print the maximum expected value Peter can get if he plays optimally. Your answer will be considered correct if the absolute or relative difference between your answer and judge's answer is less than 10−8%%ZSMJ19%%.

legend: The Arriaga Museum is going to replace its old system of codes assigned to the works with a new, clearer, and more organized one.

Some pieces are twin works. They are pairs of pieces that share exactly the same code because they are practically identical. In the new system, this must be maintained: two works that had the same old code must retain the same new code, and works with different codes cannot share one.

The works are placed in a long hallway in a fixed order that cannot be modified. From time to time, Mr. Ernesto Lafuente, the catalog inspector, walks down the hallway reviewing the works in that same order. It is much more convenient for him if, as he progresses, the codes he reads tend to appear in increasing order.

The Board wants to assign the new codes in such a way that, while respecting exactly the same groups of twin works as the old system, the number of times a greater code appears before a lesser one in the walkthrough is minimized.
Help them by constructing a code assignment that minimizes that number. The new codes must:
Maintain exactly the same groups of twin works as the old codes.
Minimize the number of pairs of positions i<j%%ZSMJ0%% where the code at position i%%ZSMJ1%% is greater than the code at position j%%ZSMJ2%%, known as an inversion.
If there are multiple optimal solutions, any of them will be valid.
input: The first line contains an integer T%%ZSMJ3%%, the number of cases to process.
The first line of each case contains n%%ZSMJ4%%, the number of works placed in the hallway.

The second line contains n%%ZSMJ5%% positive integers a1,a2,…,an%%ZSMJ6%%, where ai%%ZSMJ7%% is the old code of the work located at position i%%ZSMJ8%% in the hallway. Each value appears at most twice.
output: For each case, you must print a line with n%%ZSMJ9%% positive integers, b1,b2,…,bn%%ZSMJ10%%, representing the new codes assigned to the works to minimize the number of inversions, in the same order as in the hallway. If there are multiple optimal assignments, you can print any of them.
note: The sum of n%%ZSMJ13%% across all cases will be at most 105%%ZSMJ14%%.
1≤ai,bi≤n%%ZSMJ15%%

problems.hint: Find the necessary condition.

legend: Marisa has n%%ZSMJ0%% magic books placed on a shelf, all of them volumes from the same collection. Each book has an associated number within the collection. Initially, the book in position i%%ZSMJ1%% on the shelf is volume number ai%%ZSMJ2%% of the collection, for 1≤i≤n%%ZSMJ3%%.

Since the magic books are very delicate, they can only be moved using the following operation. Two indices 1≤i<j≤n%%ZSMJ4%% are chosen such that the volume numbers of the books in positions i,i+1,…,j%%ZSMJ5%% on the shelf are pairwise coprime∗%%ZSMJ6%%; and the order of the books in positions i,i+1,…,j%%ZSMJ7%% is reversed. That is, the book in position i+r%%ZSMJ8%% would move to position j−r%%ZSMJ9%% for each 0≤r≤j−i%%ZSMJ10%%.

Help Marisa decide if she can sort the books on the shelf using this operation as many times as she wants. We say that the books on the shelf are sorted if the volume numbers form a non-decreasing sequence from the book in position 1%%ZSMJ11%% to the book in position n%%ZSMJ12%%.
∗%%ZSMJ13%%We recall that two integers are coprime if their greatest common divisor is 1. We say that several numbers are pairwise coprime if any pair of them is coprime.

The next line contains n%%ZSMJ16%% integers a1,a2,…,an%%ZSMJ17%%, where ai%%ZSMJ18%% is the volume number of the book initially in position i%%ZSMJ19%%. Note that a1,a2,…,an%%ZSMJ20%% do not have to be pairwise distinct.
output: For each test case, print on one line the word "YES" when it is possible to sort the books, and the word "NO" when it is not possible.

problems.hint: What can the operations do?

legend: While explaining the solutions to the Math Contest problems at the Third Winter Training Camp at ESCOM, Iván came up with the following idea to challenge the participants:
You are given two big numbers A%%ZSMJ0%% and B%%ZSMJ1%% that does not contain the digit 0%%ZSMJ2%%. These numbers can be modified by performing two types of operations:

Swap two adjacent digits in one of the numbers. For example, if B=2468%%ZSMJ3%%, performing this type of operation can result in B=4268%%ZSMJ4%%, B=2648%%ZSMJ5%%, or B=2486%%ZSMJ6%%. Note that you can perform this operation on A%%ZSMJ7%% as well.

Swap the least significant digits of A%%ZSMJ8%% and B%%ZSMJ9%%. For example, if A=348%%ZSMJ10%% and B=1234%%ZSMJ11%%, performing this type of operation will result in A=344%%ZSMJ12%% and B=1238%%ZSMJ13%%.
Find the maximum value of A+B%%ZSMJ14%% that you can get by performing the operations above any number of times and in any order. As this number might be huge, print it modulo 998244353%%ZSMJ15%%.

output: Print a single integer – the maximum value of A+B%%ZSMJ20%% modulo 998244353%%ZSMJ21%%.

legend: An experiment at the Large Hadron Collider is being set up to test phase properties of various different particles. There are N%%ZSMJ0%% filters arranged in a circle, where the i%%ZSMJ1%%-th filter allows particles with a phase less than or equal to its limit Ai%%ZSMJ2%% to pass.

An experiment begins with the release of a particle at the position of the i%%ZSMJ3%%-th filter, with an initial phase set to Ai%%ZSMJ4%%. When passing through filter i%%ZSMJ5%%, including the first one, the particle:
Is filtered out if the phase of the particle is greater than the limit Ai%%ZSMJ6%%, ending the experiment.
Otherwise, the particle passes through the filter, increases its phase by K%%ZSMJ7%%, and moves to the next filter on the right, the (imod%%ZSMJ8%%-th filter.

We want to simulate the result of this experiment to compare with the results verified empirically. To achieve this, we need to create a vector B_i%%ZSMJ9%% of size N%%ZSMJ10%%, where B_i%%ZSMJ11%% (1 \leq B_i \leq N%%ZSMJ12%%) is the position of the filter that stopped the particle that started at position i%%ZSMJ13%%.
input: The first line contains two integers N%%ZSMJ14%% (1 \leq N \leq 2 \cdot 10^5%%ZSMJ15%%) and K%%ZSMJ16%% (1 \leq K \leq 10^9%%ZSMJ17%%). The second line contains N%%ZSMJ18%% integers A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_N%%ZSMJ19%% (-10^9 \leq A_i \leq 10^9%%ZSMJ20%%).
output: Print a line containing N%%ZSMJ21%% integers B_1, B_2, \ldots, B_N%%ZSMJ22%%.

legend: Bessie is trying to convert a number X%%ZSMJ0%% to Y%%ZSMJ1%%.

In one operation, Bessie can choose an integer M%%ZSMJ2%% (M≥1%%ZSMJ3%%) and round X%%ZSMJ4%% to the nearest multiple of M%%ZSMJ5%%. If X%%ZSMJ6%% is exactly in the middle of two multiples of M%%ZSMJ7%%, it is rounded up. Note that 0%%ZSMJ8%% is a multiple of every number.
What is the least number of operations Bessie needs to perform to convert X%%ZSMJ9%% to Y%%ZSMJ10%%? Output this number, or −1%%ZSMJ11%% if it is impossible.

Each of the next T%%ZSMJ14%% lines contains two integers X%%ZSMJ15%% and Y%%ZSMJ16%% (1≤X,Y≤109%%ZSMJ17%%) — the initial number and the target number.

note: In the first testcase of the first sample, X=2%%ZSMJ19%% and Y=5%%ZSMJ20%%. Bessie can perform the following 2%%ZSMJ21%% operations:
Choose M=4%%ZSMJ22%%. The multiples of 4%%ZSMJ23%% are 0,4,8,…%%ZSMJ24%%. X=2%%ZSMJ25%% is exactly in the middle of 0%%ZSMJ26%% and 4%%ZSMJ27%%, so it rounds up to 4%%ZSMJ28%%. Now X=4%%ZSMJ29%%.
Choose M=5%%ZSMJ30%%. The multiples of 5%%ZSMJ31%% are 0,5,10,…%%ZSMJ32%%. The nearest multiple to 4%%ZSMJ33%% is 5%%ZSMJ34%%. Now X=5%%ZSMJ35%%.
It can be proven that it is impossible to do this in fewer than 2%%ZSMJ36%% operations.
In the second testcase of the first sample, X=6%%ZSMJ37%% and Y=4%%ZSMJ38%%.
Choose M=5%%ZSMJ39%%. X=6%%ZSMJ40%% is nearest to 5%%ZSMJ41%%. Now X=5%%ZSMJ42%%.
Choose M=4%%ZSMJ43%%. X=5%%ZSMJ44%% is nearest to 4%%ZSMJ45%%. Now X=4%%ZSMJ46%%.
It can be proven that it is impossible to do this in fewer than 2%%ZSMJ47%% operations.

legend: For two positive integers l,r%%ZSMJ0%%, f(l,r)%%ZSMJ1%% is defined as the number of ordered pairs (a,b)%%ZSMJ2%% such that l≤a+b≤r%%ZSMJ3%%, a%%ZSMJ4%% and b%%ZSMJ5%% are positive, and gcd(a,b)=p%%ZSMJ6%%, where p%%ZSMJ7%% is a prime number.

legend: You are organizing a tournament for n%%ZSMJ0%% gladiators. The i%%ZSMJ1%%-th gladiator has a strength level ai%%ZSMJ2%%.
The tournament consists of exactly n−1%%ZSMJ3%% duels. In each duel:

Two distinct gladiators are chosen uniformly at random from those remaining in the tournament. Let their strengths be x%%ZSMJ4%% and y%%ZSMJ5%%. Note that two distinct gladiators may have equal strengths.
The duel generates a brutality of |x−y|%%ZSMJ6%%.
One of the two gladiators is chosen uniformly at random to be eliminated, while the other remains in the tournament.
The process continues until only one gladiator remains. Compute the expected total brutality of the tournament modulo 998244353%%ZSMJ7%%.
input: The first line contains a single integer t%%ZSMJ8%% (1≤t≤104%%ZSMJ9%%) — the number of test cases.
The first line of each test case contains an integer n%%ZSMJ10%% (2≤n≤3⋅105%%ZSMJ11%%) — the number of gladiators.
The second line contains n%%ZSMJ12%% integers a1,a2,…,an%%ZSMJ13%% (−109≤ai≤109%%ZSMJ14%%) — the strength levels of the gladiators.
It is guaranteed that the sum of n%%ZSMJ15%% over all test cases does not exceed 3⋅105%%ZSMJ16%%.
output: For each test case, output a single integer — the expected total brutality modulo 998244353%%ZSMJ17%%.

Formally, let M=998244353%%ZSMJ18%%. It can be shown that the answer can be expressed as an irreducible fraction pq%%ZSMJ19%%, where p%%ZSMJ20%% and q%%ZSMJ21%% are integers and q \not\equiv 0 \pmod M%%ZSMJ22%%. Output the integer equal to p \cdot q^{-1} \pmod M%%ZSMJ23%%.
note: In the first test case, let the gladiators be A%%ZSMJ24%%, B%%ZSMJ25%%, C%%ZSMJ26%% with strengths 1%%ZSMJ27%%, 4%%ZSMJ28%%, 2%%ZSMJ29%% respectively. The tournament tree looks like:
![](https://espresso.codeforces.com/cb3afb77cc2a81ca975e966361cc49df7e5cb7b6.png)

Here, b%%ZSMJ30%% denotes brutality, -X%%ZSMJ31%% on an edge means gladiator X%%ZSMJ32%% is eliminated, and the boxed numbers are the total brutality for each scenario. There are 6%%ZSMJ33%% equally likely scenarios, so the expected total brutality is: \frac{5 + 4 + 3 + 4 + 3 + 5}{6} = \frac{24}{6} = 4.%%ZSMJ34%%

statement.title: J. The Power of the Sun

legend: Dr. Otto Octavius is a brilliant nuclear physicist working on his life's work: a sustainable fusion power source. He claims to have "the power of the sun, in the palm of his hand" with his new Infinite Factorial Reactor.
The reactor consists of n%%ZSMJ0%% fusion cores lined up in a row, indexed from 1%%ZSMJ1%% to n%%ZSMJ2%%. Initially, the i%%ZSMJ3%%-th core holds an energy level of ai%%ZSMJ4%%.
Octavius uses his mechanical arms to conduct q%%ZSMJ5%% operations. In each operation, he interacts with a specific range of cores [l,r]%%ZSMJ6%%. The operations are of two types:

If every subset of creatures of both mages always has the same strength, the draw is declared.

It has turned out, that if k=1%%ZSMJ2%% or k=3%%ZSMJ3%%, the first mage has strictly greater chances to win, and if k=2%%ZSMJ4%%, the second mage has. You have to give an example of sets of creatures of the first and the second mages.

The first mage has three creatures, their strengths are 1, 2 and 3. The second mage has three creatures, all their strengths are equal to 2.

If k=1%%ZSMJ15%%, the second mage always has fixed strength 2. If the first mage summons the creature with the strength 2, the process repeats. If he summons the creature with the strength 3, he wins, and with the strength 1 — loses. The probability of the first mage to win is 0.5, but the problem requires the first mage to have strictly better chances.

If k=2%%ZSMJ16%%, the second mage always has strength 4. The first mage can summon the following subsets of creatures: (1, 2), (1, 3), (2, 3). If it is (1, 2), the first mage loses (as 3 < 4), if it is (1, 3) — the game starts again (as 4 = 4), and if it's (2, 3) — he wins. The resulting probability is again 0.5, but the second mage should have better chances in this case.

If k=3%%ZSMJ17%%, the subsets of the first and second mages are always (1, 2, 3) and (2, 2, 2). They have equal strengths, and we got infinite game restarts. According to the rules, the draw is declared in this case, so the probability of the first mage winning is not greater again.

**提示 1：** 找到一个简单一点的形式。

考虑两个数组长度都为 $3$ 。此时暴力一点的方式可以直接枚举所有组合看是否满足要求。我们这里说下手动构造的可能方法。

先假设两个是 $a,a,b$ 和 $c,c,d$ 的形式。同时 $a\lt b$ ， $c\lt d$ 。

这样有 $4$ 个自由度，组成三个不等式蛮可能是可以有解的。

如果 $c$ 比 $a,b$ 都小，第一个条件自动满足。

如果 $a+b\gt c+d$ ，那么第二个条件也满足。

如果 $2a+b\gt 2c+d$ ，第三个条件也满足。

这个凑解就容易多了。

### 具体代码如下——

Python 做法如下——

```Python []
def main(): 
    print(3)
    print(3, 3, 4)
    print(3)
    print(1, 1, 7)
```

C++ 做法如下——

```cpp []
int main() {
	ios_base::sync_with_stdio(false);
	cin.tie(0);
	cout.tie(0);

	cout << "3\n3 3 4\n3\n1 1 7";

	return 0;
}
```

A topological ordering of a directed graph G=(V,E)%%ZSMJ41%% is a linear ordering (i.e., permutation) of its vertices such that for every directed edge (u,v)∈E%%ZSMJ42%% from vertex u%%ZSMJ43%% to vertex v%%ZSMJ44%%, u%%ZSMJ45%% comes before v%%ZSMJ46%% in the ordering. aj=bj%%ZSMJ54%% for all j<i%%ZSMJ55%%.

legend: Bessie needs to produce energy as possible in her mooclear reactor. She has n%%ZSMJ0%% different particles.

legend: One of the longest-running events of the Office Olympics is the Toilet High Jump. This event was initially introduced to the Olympics by Thomas Crapper in 1905 as a means to get his employees more excited to sell toilets. The event rewards the ability to jump to very tall heights, with the gold medal being awarded to the employee who can jump the highest.

The way the event is structured is as follows: The n%%ZSMJ0%% employees of Crapper & Co. each have predetermined "jump heights" ji%%ZSMJ1%% (measured in units) that determine the maximum height they can jump. The event will consist of m%%ZSMJ2%% rounds. Initially, there is a sequence of k%%ZSMJ3%% tiles containing exactly one toilet each. During the i%%ZSMJ4%%-th round, Thomas will choose two indices li%%ZSMJ5%% and ri%%ZSMJ6%% (subject to 1≤li≤ri≤k%%ZSMJ7%%) and then an integer xi%%ZSMJ8%% and stack exactly xi%%ZSMJ9%% unique toilets upon the existing toilets in the tiles li,li+1,…,ri%%ZSMJ10%%. That is to say, the number of toilets within each of the tiles in the range [li,ri]%%ZSMJ11%% will increase by xi%%ZSMJ12%%.

Importantly, each toilet has a height of 1 unit, and when a new toilet is added to a tile, the height of the toilets in that tile increases by 1 unit. Once the toilets in the i%%ZSMJ13%%-th round have been added, each of the n%%ZSMJ14%% employees will attempt to jump from tile 1%%ZSMJ15%% to tile k%%ZSMJ16%%. Initially, each employee will be standing atop the pile of toilets in tile 1%%ZSMJ17%%, and to jump from tile i%%ZSMJ18%% to tile i+1%%ZSMJ19%% (assuming the current heights of toilets in tiles i%%ZSMJ20%% and i+1%%ZSMJ21%% are hi%%ZSMJ22%% and hi+1%%ZSMJ23%%, respectively), the employee must have a jump height of at least max(0,hi+1−hi)%%ZSMJ24%%. Obviously, it could be the case that some employees cannot finish the course and won't earn a point for that specific round.

As the referee of the event, your job is simple. You must carefully observe each round and determine how many employees earn points after each of the m%%ZSMJ25%% rounds. Then, you must report this information to Thomas Crapper so that he may determine the winner (and thus the employee(s) who will receive the gold medal). Note that toilets are not reset between rounds, that is, added toilets remain stacked in their respective tiles.
input: The input will begin with a line containing three space-separated integers, n%%ZSMJ26%% (1≤n≤105%%ZSMJ27%%), m%%ZSMJ28%% (1≤m≤105%%ZSMJ29%%), and k%%ZSMJ30%% (1≤k≤105%%ZSMJ31%%) as described above.
The next line of input will consist of n%%ZSMJ32%% space-separated integers ji%%ZSMJ33%% (1≤ji≤1018%%ZSMJ34%%), denoting the jump heights of the n%%ZSMJ35%% employees.

The next m%%ZSMJ36%% lines of input will each describe one of the rounds of the event. Each of these m%%ZSMJ37%% lines will consist of three space-separated integers li%%ZSMJ38%%, ri%%ZSMJ39%% (1≤li≤ri≤k%%ZSMJ40%%), and xi%%ZSMJ41%% (1≤xi≤2⋅109%%ZSMJ42%%). These three integers describe the i%%ZSMJ43%%-th round of the event as explained above.

legend: Thomas has decided today is the day that Crapper & Co. bands together and embarks on an odyssey! That is, an odyssey aboard rolling chairs across the office...

legend: This is the easy version. The difference between the easy version and the hard version is the constraints.

legend: Every year, mathematicians and computer scientists from around the globe gather for the prestigious Inversion Counting Puzzle Contest (ICPC). For the next ICPC, the organizers had prepared the following challenge: given a string S%%ZSMJ0%% consisting of lowercase letters, count the number of inversions in it. An inversion is a pair of indices i<j%%ZSMJ1%% such that Si%%ZSMJ2%% (the letter at position i%%ZSMJ3%%) comes after Sj%%ZSMJ4%% in the alphabet.

However, just last month, a group of outstanding researchers devised a sophisticated algorithm that can count the inversions in a string extremely fast. While this was great news for the advancement of science, it has been a nightmare for the ICPC staff, since their planned challenge is now obsolete.

This issue escalated to the head problem setter, who then presented a clever idea. Instead of simply receiving a string S%%ZSMJ5%%, they should ask participants to repeat this string N%%ZSMJ6%% times before counting the inversions. legend: This is an interactive problem.

Chloe wants to test her sorting skills. She has n%%ZSMJ0%% cards with distinct integers from 1%%ZSMJ1%% to n%%ZSMJ2%% written on them. She asks her little brother Connor to first blindfold her and then arrange all cards in a row in some order. Positions of cards are numbered from 1%%ZSMJ3%% to n%%ZSMJ4%% from left to right.

Chloe doesn't know the order of the cards, but she wants to sort them, so that the leftmost card has number 1%%ZSMJ5%% and the rightmost card has number n%%ZSMJ6%% on it. Formally, for each i%%ZSMJ7%% she wants the card on position i%%ZSMJ8%% to have number i%%ZSMJ9%% on it. To achieve the goal, Chloe can ask Connor to do one or more operations.

Each operation can be denoted by two integers posi%%ZSMJ10%% and posj%%ZSMJ11%% (1≤posi<posj≤n%%ZSMJ12%%). Connor looks at the cards on positions posi%%ZSMJ13%% and posj%%ZSMJ14%%, and if the card on position posi%%ZSMJ15%% has a bigger number than the card on position posj%%ZSMJ16%%, he swaps them. Otherwise, he does nothing. Connor also tells Chloe if he swapped the cards or not.
To make the game more interesting, after every 2n%%ZSMJ17%% operations Connor chooses two distinct cards uniformly at random and swaps them without telling anything to Chloe.
If after some of Chloe's operations all cards become sorted, Chloe wins. Help Chloe to sort all cards using at most 10 000%%ZSMJ18%% operations.
Interaction
Your program should start by reading a single integer n%%ZSMJ19%% (2≤n≤50%%ZSMJ20%%) — the number of cards.

Your program can ask to do the specified operation one or more times. To do the operation, your program should print its description formatted as "posi%%ZSMJ21%% posj%%ZSMJ22%%" — two distinct numbers denoting the positions of cards (1≤posi<posj≤n%%ZSMJ23%%). Remember to flush the output after printing each operation description. Then your program should read the outcome of the operation — it will be a single word SWAPPED if the cards were swapped, or a single word STAYED if nothing changed.

If instead of an operation outcome your program receives a single word WIN, it means that the cards have become sorted. Your program should terminate silently after that, it is not allowed to output any extra operations.

After every 2n%%ZSMJ24%% operations two distinct cards are chosen randomly and swapped without telling anything to your program. Each pair of cards has equal probability to be chosen. This swap is not counted as an operation.

legend: The future is here! The Boxes And Parcels Centre has decided to start delivering parcels using drones. Being a BrAinPort Company, naturally the first deliveries will be to Eindhoven.

To keep the flight logic simple, the first prototype will only deliver to the roofs of the tallest buildings. After take-off, the drone will take a $$$w\times h$$$ ($$$1 \leq w\leq 10\,000$$$, $$$1\leq h\leq 10^{18}$$$) photo of the skyline, as shown in Figure 1. You have been tasked with the problem of determining the location and height of the tallest building in this photo, so that the drone knows where to go.

You have access to a classifier that can determine for each pixel whether it is "sky" or "building". You can use this multiple times for different pixels. To avoid unnecessary delays, you may run the classifier at most $$$12\,000$$$ times.

It is guaranteed that the buildings will not contain any hovering parts: whenever a pixel that is not on the bottom row of the photo is classified as building, the pixels below it will also be classified as building.
![](https://espresso.codeforces.com/e415600b72bda53369e257afb0a5bfc7ffd04852.png)
Interaction

This is an interactive problem. Your submission will be run against an interactor, which reads from the standard output of your submission and writes to the standard input of your submission. This interaction needs to follow a specific protocol:
The interactor first sends one line with two integers $$$w$$$ and $$$h$$$ ($$$1\leq w\leq 10\,000$$$, $$$1\leq h\leq 10^{18}$$$), the width and height of the photo in pixels.

Then, your program should make at most $$$12\,000$$$ queries to find the highest building. Each query is made by printing one line of the form "? $$$x$$$ $$$y$$$" ($$$1\leq x\leq w$$$, $$$1\leq y\leq h$$$). The interactor will respond with either "sky" or "building", indicating the classification of the pixel at coordinates $$$(x, y)$$$.

When you have determined the $$$x$$$-coordinate of one of the highest buildings and its height $$$y$$$, print one line of the form "! $$$x$$$ $$$y$$$", after which the interaction will stop. Printing the answer does not count as a query.
The interactor is not adaptive: the skyline is fixed up front, and does not depend on your queries.
If there are multiple valid solutions, you may output any one of them.
Make sure you flush the buffer after each write.
A testing tool is provided to help you develop your solution.
Using more than $$$12\,000$$$ queries will result in a wrong answer.

legend: Tim the Busy Beaver has signed up for a pistol class in order to pass their PE requirement and wants to be an elite marksman. legend: Busy Beaver is making a new language for his linguistics class! He has already decided that his language will have an alphabet whose letters are the integers 1,…,NM%%ZSMJ0%% in that order; now he wants to make some words for the language.

legend: Nick has always struggled with maintaining habits. The problem is that he just can't stop maintaining them. If Nick does something K%%ZSMJ0%% times in a row, he has to keep doing it forever.

legend: You are probably familiar with the classic problem of finding the longest increasing subsequence in an array. Let a%%ZSMJ0%% be an array consisting of n%%ZSMJ1%% integers. A subsequence i1<i2<…<ik%%ZSMJ2%% is called increasing if ai1<ai2<…<aik%%ZSMJ3%%. The longest increasing subsequence is the increasing subsequence of maximum length. Of course, we will not ask you to solve the classic problem; you will have to solve its more complicated version...

Initially, there is an empty array a%%ZSMJ4%%. Then, the numbers 1,2,…,n%%ZSMJ5%% are added to the array in this order. The number i%%ZSMJ6%% is added to the array at position pi%%ZSMJ7%%. Positions in the array are numbered with integers from 1%%ZSMJ8%% to k%%ZSMJ9%%, where k%%ZSMJ10%% is the current size of the array. When adding an element at position p%%ZSMJ11%% in an array of size k%%ZSMJ12%%, all elements that previously had positions from p%%ZSMJ13%% to k%%ZSMJ14%% are shifted one position to the right, and the current element is added to the freed space.

The second line contains n%%ZSMJ17%% integers p1,p2,…,pn%%ZSMJ18%% (1≤pi≤i%%ZSMJ19%%) — pi%%ZSMJ20%% denotes the position where element i%%ZSMJ21%% is added.

legend: A subarray of an array is a contiguous portion of the array. A partition of an array into subarrays is a collection of subarrays that cover all the array without overlaps (each element in the array belongs to exactly one subarray). For instance, if A=[3,1,4,1,5]%%ZSMJ0%% is an array, [3,1,4]%%ZSMJ1%% and [1,5]%%ZSMJ2%% form a partition of A%%ZSMJ3%% into subarrays, while [3,4,5]%%ZSMJ4%% is not a subarray of A%%ZSMJ5%%.

Those are standard definitions that you may have read elsewhere. So, what's new here? Well, a few more definitions follow. Given an array A%%ZSMJ6%% of integers, a subarray [Ai,Ai+1,…,Aj]%%ZSMJ7%% of A%%ZSMJ8%% is called a mountain if there exists an index k%%ZSMJ9%% such that i<k<j%%ZSMJ10%%, the subarray from Ai%%ZSMJ11%% to Ak%%ZSMJ12%% is non-decreasing, and the subarray from Ak%%ZSMJ13%% to Aj%%ZSMJ14%% is non-increasing. In simple words, the values in the subarray "go up" until index k%%ZSMJ15%% and then "go down", resembling a mountain. Note that a subarray with fewer than three elements cannot be a mountain.

An array of integers is called a beautiful mountain chain if it can be partitioned into mountains, each of them having the same number of elements, except for the last mountain which may have fewer elements.

As an example, [5,10,4,1,3,2]%%ZSMJ16%% is a beautiful mountain chain because it can be partitioned into [5,10,4]%%ZSMJ17%% and [1,3,2]%%ZSMJ18%%, being both mountains that have the same number of elements. Another example is the array [5,10,4,4,10,20,30,20,2,3,1]%%ZSMJ19%%, which is also a beautiful mountain chain because it can be partitioned into [5,10,4,4]%%ZSMJ20%%, [10,20,30,20]%%ZSMJ21%% and [2,3,1]%%ZSMJ22%%.
Given an array of positive integers, where some values can be missing, determine if it is possible to complete the array with positive integers such that it becomes a beautiful mountain chain.
input: The first line contains an integer N%%ZSMJ23%% (3≤N≤105%%ZSMJ24%%) indicating the number of elements in the array. The second line contains N%%ZSMJ25%% integers A1,A2,…,AN%%ZSMJ26%% (Ai=−1%%ZSMJ27%% or 1≤Ai≤109%%ZSMJ28%% for i=1,2,…,N%%ZSMJ29%%), where Ai=−1%%ZSMJ30%% indicates that the i%%ZSMJ31%%-th element of the array needs to be determined, and a positive value is the actual i%%ZSMJ32%%-th element of the array.

legend: You are given an array a%%ZSMJ0%% of n%%ZSMJ1%% integers. You then perform the following process k%%ZSMJ2%% times.

For each 1≤j≤n%%ZSMJ5%%, move aj%%ZSMJ6%% one unit closer to ai%%ZSMJ7%%. Formally, for each j%%ZSMJ8%%,  If aj<ai%%ZSMJ9%%, increment aj%%ZSMJ10%% by 1%%ZSMJ11%%
If aj>ai%%ZSMJ12%%, decrement aj%%ZSMJ13%% by 1%%ZSMJ14%%
If aj=ai%%ZSMJ15%%, do not modify the value of aj%%ZSMJ16%%.
After performing this process k%%ZSMJ17%% times, you select an integer i%%ZSMJ18%% where 1≤i≤n%%ZSMJ19%% uniformly at random. What is the expected value of ai%%ZSMJ20%%?

It can be shown that this value can be represented as PQ%%ZSMJ21%% where P%%ZSMJ22%% and Q%%ZSMJ23%% are coprime integers and Q \not\equiv 0 \mod 10^9+7%%ZSMJ24%%. Print the value of P\cdot Q^{-1}%%ZSMJ25%% modulo 10^9+7%%ZSMJ26%%.
input: The first line of the input contains a single integer t%%ZSMJ27%% (1\le t\le 10^4%%ZSMJ28%%) — the number of test cases.
The first line of each test case contains two integers n%%ZSMJ29%% and k%%ZSMJ30%% (1\le n,k \le 2\cdot 10^5%%ZSMJ31%%) — the length of the array and the number of operations you will perform.
The second line of each test case will contain n%%ZSMJ32%% integers a_1, a_2, \cdots a_n%%ZSMJ33%% (1 \le a_i \le 10^9%%ZSMJ34%%) — the initial array a%%ZSMJ35%%.

output: For each test case, output a single line containing the expected value of a_i%%ZSMJ39%% at the end of this process, modulo 10^9+7%%ZSMJ40%% as described above.
note: In the first sample case, since all elements of a%%ZSMJ41%% are initially equal, none of them will change after any of the k=5%%ZSMJ42%% operations. Therefore, the final array will be [8, 8, 8]%%ZSMJ43%%, so the expected value of a random element of the final array is 8%%ZSMJ44%%.
In the second sample case, there is a 50\%%%ZSMJ45%% chance of choosing i = 1%%ZSMJ46%% in the operation, and a 50\%%%ZSMJ47%% chance of choosing i = 2%%ZSMJ48%%.

If i = 1%%ZSMJ49%% is chosen, all elements of the array will move closer to a_1 = 10%%ZSMJ50%%, so a%%ZSMJ51%% will go from [10, 11]%%ZSMJ52%% to [10, 10]%%ZSMJ53%%. The expected value of a random element of this array is 10%%ZSMJ54%%.

If i = 2%%ZSMJ55%% is chosen, all elements of the array will move closer to a_2 = 11%%ZSMJ56%%, so a%%ZSMJ57%% will go from [10, 11]%%ZSMJ58%% to [11, 11]%%ZSMJ59%%. The expected value of a random element of this array is 11%%ZSMJ60%%.

So there is a 50\%%%ZSMJ61%% chance of the expected value being 10%%ZSMJ62%%, and a 50\%%%ZSMJ63%% chance of it being 11%%ZSMJ64%%. Therefore, the final expected value is 10.5 = \frac{21}{2}%%ZSMJ65%%, which is equivalent to 5000000014%%ZSMJ66%% modulo 10^9+7%%ZSMJ67%%.

legend: Usually everyone associates the New Year with a Christmas tree and a festive table, but students associate the New Year with exams session. It was December 31, and second-year students signed up for the exam.

Teachers need all students to have the opportunity to take the exam, so some students may have to be moved to another day. Teachers can choose any number of students and assign each of them to take the exam on any day.
If a student wanted to take the exam on the i%%ZSMJ4%%-th day, and the teachers eventually moved it to the j%%ZSMJ5%%-th day, then dissatisfaction of this student will be equal to |i−j|%%ZSMJ6%%.

6,14,70,1%%ZSMJ23%% — initial schedule of students;

legend: A Dyson Sphere is a theoretical construction around the sun or another star, that captures the entire energy output of the star. Science fiction writers have speculated that advanced civilizations will eventually build such a sphere, as the energy demands of such a society continue to grow without bounds. In our three-dimensional space, Dyson spheres are still in the realm of fiction. {Dy & Son}, the main energy company of your dimensional neighbours, has tasked you with carrying out a feasibility study in the two-dimensional world of Flatland.

{Dy & Son} has developed a modular Dyson Circle. It consists of independent square Dyson Units that can chain together to form a closed loop that gathers energy. Your task is to figure out how many of these Dyson units they actually need to enclose the star or stars they are interested in. Note that they want a single Dyson Circle, not a separate one for each star.

For convenience, both the stars {Dy & Son} wants to enclose and the Dyson Units used for this are modeled as squares of exactly 1%%ZSMJ0%% by 1%%ZSMJ1%% Intergalactic Unit, aligned to the Intergalactic Coordinate System. ![](https://espresso.codeforces.com/4636991984855402273c73f61e930ed54fde49f0.png)

Formally, select some squares in the plane to turn into Dyson Units, such that the remaining squares can be split into inside and outside squares. All the stars must be inside squares. The inside squares must form a contiguous region (connected via edges) and not connect to the outside squares (via edges). The outside squares form a contiguous region stretching off to infinity.

n%%ZSMJ4%% lines, each containing two integers x%%ZSMJ5%% and y%%ZSMJ6%% (−106≤x,y≤106%%ZSMJ7%%), the location of the center of a star.
output: Output the least number of Dyson units required to capture the energy of all stars in the input.

legend: Given a tree consisting of $$$n$$$ nodes.
Is there a walk that visits all the nodes of the tree at least once and at most twice?
Note that the node you start the walk at is considered visited at the beginning.
A walk is a sequence of nodes $$$v_1, v_2, \dots, v_k$$$ such that for each $$$i$$$ ($$$1 \le i  \lt  k$$$), $$$v_i$$$ and $$$v_{i + 1}$$$ are connected by an edge.
input: The first line of the input contains a single integer $$$t$$$ ($$$1 \le t \le 10^5$$$) — the number of testcases.
The first line of each testcase contains a single integer $$$n$$$ ($$$2 \le n \le 2 \cdot 10^5$$$) — the number of nodes in the tree.

Each of the following $$$n - 1$$$ lines of each testcase consists of two space-separated integers $$$u$$$ and $$$v$$$ ($$$1 \le u, v \le n$$$) denoting an edge between nodes $$$u$$$ and $$$v$$$ in the tree.
It is guaranteed that the given edges form a tree.
It is guaranteed that the sum of $$$n$$$ over all the testcases will not exceed $$$2 \cdot 10^5$$$.
output: For each testcase, print "YES" (without quotes) if there exists a walk that satisfies the conditions, otherwise print "NO" (without quotes).
You can output "YES" and "NO" in any case (for example, strings "yEs", "yes", "Yes" and "YES" will be recognized as a positive response).
note: Explanation of the first testcase: we can start at node $$$1$$$ then go to node $$$2$$$ and stop there.
Explanation of the second testcase: a valid walk may look like this: $$$5$$$ — $$$3$$$ — $$$4$$$ — $$$3$$$ — $$$1$$$ — $$$2$$$ — $$$1$$$.
Notice that it is not necessary to start at node $$$1$$$.
Nodes $$$1$$$ and $$$3$$$ were visited twice, whereas nodes $$$2$$$, $$$4$$$, and $$$5$$$ were visited once. Thus, each node is visited at least once and at most twice and the walk is valid.
Explanation of the third testcase: it can be shown that there does not exist a walk that satisfies the conditions.

legend: Shanto has finally decided that it's time for him to get married!

Although it took a while for him to reach this decision, it didn't take long for the news to spread like wildfire. Soon, Shanto's phone started to ring nonstop, with n%%ZSMJ0%% girls requesting to chat with him, each seeing him as a perfect life partner. Being overwhelmed, Shanto devised an algorithm to find his favorite girl.
Here's his plan:
Tomorrow, Shanto will chat with the girls one by one in the order they called.
For every girl, Shanto will calculate the happiness he feels during the chat.
At any point, Shanto will keep track of the favorite girl he's met so far.
After chatting with the first girl, she's automatically the favorite girl (for now).
For subsequent girls:      If the happiness Shanto feels chatting with her is less than that of the current favorite girl, he will stick with his favorite girl.
If it's greater, she will become the new favorite girl.
If it's equal, Shanto will flip an unbiased coin. If the coin lands on heads, he will stick to his current favorite girl. Otherwise, this girl will become the new favorite girl.
If Shanto can finish chatting with all the girls, he will choose his favorite girl to become his wife.

However, at any point, if Shanto chats with k%%ZSMJ1%% consecutive girls and no girl strictly surpasses his maximum happiness, he'll cancel the rest of the dates and go to sleep. In this case, his current favorite girl gets to become "Mrs. Shanto"!

Being an honest boy, Shanto shares all the details about the algorithm with the girls. But here's a twist: Shanto himself doesn't know the value of k%%ZSMJ2%% yet. Influenced by one of his roommates, Shanto has developed a habit of making important decisions at the last moment. So, he decided to sleep on it and choose k%%ZSMJ3%% tomorrow morning.

Meanwhile, the girls, excited and anxious, started fantasizing about their chances. Some have tried to read Shanto's mind and guess the value of k%%ZSMJ4%%. Others have decided to pray for an optimal k%%ZSMJ5%% to maximize their chances. Now, they've turned to you, the only person who can predict Shanto's happiness levels, for help.
Your task is to calm their nerves by answering their queries.

Then q%%ZSMJ14%% lines follow, each containing a query of one of the following two types:
"1 i k": the i%%ZSMJ15%%-th girl (1≤i≤n)%%ZSMJ16%% asks about the probability of her becoming Shanto's wife for the given value of k(1≤k≤n)%%ZSMJ17%%.
"2 i": the i%%ZSMJ18%%-th girl (1≤i≤n)%%ZSMJ19%% asks about the optimal value of k%%ZSMJ20%% that maximizes the probability of her becoming Shanto's wife and the corresponding probability.

For each query of type 1, output one integer p(0≤p<109+7)%%ZSMJ21%%.
For each query of type 2, output two space-separated integers k(1≤k≤n)%%ZSMJ22%% and p(0≤p<109+7)%%ZSMJ23%%. If multiple values of k%%ZSMJ24%% are optimal, you can output any of them.

legend: Your friend, Mikey, has had issues recently; every week he gets food poisoning. Mikey is pretty sure that the food poisoning is from exactly one restaurant; he doesn't know which one though. Mikey wants to devise a strategy to find out. He wants to find out as quickly as possible (least number of weeks).

Mikey is willing to eat at a subset of his usual restaurants each week to find the bad restaurant (the subset can be as small or as large as needed). However, Mikey doesn't want to get food poisoning too many times, so he wants to find the bad restaurant while getting poisoned at most p times.

Note that if Mikey eats at a subset of restaurants in a given week and gets food poisoning, then the bad restaurant is in that subset; if he doesn't get food poisoning, then the bad restaurant is not in that subset. Note also that the subset of restaurants for different weeks do not have to be the same size.

Given the number of restaurants and the maximum allowable number of times to get food poisoning, determine (in the worst case) the least number of weeks needed to find out which restaurant is giving Mikey food poisoning.

legend: Machado, a renowned researcher at the BRUTE Space Agency, invented a device he believes can reveal important patterns for the trajectory of planetary orbits. This device, named "Kosmos", produced a revolutionary numeric sequence, but since it was programmed in pure C, a memory leak occurred which led to the device's self-destruction. After discovering this, Machado immediately started programming everything in Rust. Now, shaken by the loss of his invention, the only thing he remembers is that the sequence produced by the device was defined by the following recursive formula:

Kosmos had enough computational power to compute any term of this sequence from $$$1$$$ to $$$10^{18}$$$. Since the value of the term can be enormous, Machado is only interested in the remainder of this number modulo $$$998244353$$$. However, without Kosmos, Machado has no idea how to compute the $$$N$$$-th term of this sequence if $$$N$$$ is that large. Therefore, he has asked for your help.

output: Print the $$$N$$$-th term of the sequence generated by Kosmos. Since this value can be very large, print it modulo $$$998244353$$$.

legend: Alice is moving to the city of Nlogonia, and to decide where to live, she is evaluating the safety of the city.

Nlogonia is a planned city with N%%ZSMJ0%% intersections, numbered from 1%%ZSMJ1%% to N%%ZSMJ2%%, and M%%ZSMJ3%% streets. Each street connects two intersections bidirectionally. It is guaranteed that any intersection can reach all other intersections using the streets, and no two streets connect the same pair of intersections.

The government of Nlogonia publishes a danger rating Di%%ZSMJ4%% for each intersection i%%ZSMJ5%%. However, Alice thinks these ratings are insufficient because she wants to assess the safety of moving through the city, not just where she lives. So, she developed her own way to measure how dangerous the city is.

For any given path in the city, Alice defines its path risk as the maximum danger rating among all intersections on that path, including its endpoints. The risk factor between two intersections U%%ZSMJ6%% and V%%ZSMJ7%%, denoted as f(U,V)%%ZSMJ8%%, is the minimum possible path risk among all paths connecting U%%ZSMJ9%% and V%%ZSMJ10%%. By definition, the only path from an intersection U%%ZSMJ11%% to itself is the trivial path containing only U%%ZSMJ12%%, so we have f(U,U)=DU%%ZSMJ13%%. Finally, she assigns a danger score to each intersection U%%ZSMJ14%%, denoted as:
SU=N∑V=1f(U,V)%%ZSMJ15%%
In other words, the danger score of an intersection U%%ZSMJ16%% is the sum of its risk factors to every intersection in the city.
Computing these danger scores for all intersections is not easy, so Alice asks for your help!

The second line contains N%%ZSMJ23%% integers D1,D2,…,DN%%ZSMJ24%% (1≤Di≤109%%ZSMJ25%% for i=1,2,…,N%%ZSMJ26%%), where Di%%ZSMJ27%% is the danger rating of intersection i%%ZSMJ28%%.

Each of the next M%%ZSMJ29%% lines contains two integers U%%ZSMJ30%% and V%%ZSMJ31%% (1≤U,V≤N%%ZSMJ32%% and U≠V%%ZSMJ33%%), indicating that there is a two-way street between intersections U%%ZSMJ34%% and V%%ZSMJ35%%.
It is guaranteed that there is at most one street between each pair of intersections and that any intersection can be reached from any other using one or more streets.
output: Output a single line with N%%ZSMJ36%% integers S1,S2,…,SN%%ZSMJ37%%, that is, the danger scores of all the intersections.

legend: Akari, also known as Light Up, is a logic puzzle played on a rectangular grid. The player places light bulbs in empty cells until the entire grid is illuminated.

A light bulb lights up its own cell and all cells along the horizontal and vertical directions until its light hits an obstacle or the edge of the grid. No two light bulbs should be illuminated by each other. There are clue cells in the original rules indicating exactly how many bulbs must be placed in adjacent cells. However, determining whether a puzzle is solvable has been proven to be NP-complete.

![](https://espresso.codeforces.com/02c121aa8b47d1f39998ec1ccf53c57b2bf8d7bc.png)

output: Mark the light bulbs you placed with the letter 'L' and output the final configuration in the same format as the given puzzle in the input. If there are multiple solutions, print any of them. It is guaranteed that at least one solution exists for the given input.

legend: Iceberg House, a trading house, is a highly desirable workplace for young scholars thanks to its renowned reputation throughout the markets. Each year, Yessine receives a vast pool of apprenticeship seekers. In the past, he would select candidates arbitrarily. However, this year, he has learned from travelers along the Silk Road that trading houses with diverse knowledge and skills are more successful in negotiating profitable deals with merchants from distant lands.

To enhance diversity, Yessine has identified a list of n%%ZSMJ0%% skills. Each candidate has a proficiency score for each skill, ranging from 1%%ZSMJ1%% (lowest proficiency) to m%%ZSMJ2%% (highest proficiency).

To ensure a diverse selection, Yessine will choose candidates such that no applicant is more skilled than another. However, if two or more candidates are equally skilled, then Yessine will only select one of them.

A candidate A%%ZSMJ3%% is more skilled than B%%ZSMJ4%% if, for every skill, candidate A%%ZSMJ5%% has a proficiency score greater than or equal to candidate B%%ZSMJ6%%, and for at least one skill, candidate A%%ZSMJ7%% has a strictly higher proficiency score. Two candidates are equally skilled if they have exactly the same proficiency scores for all skills.
Yessine wants to maximize the number of young scholars while still adhering to the selection criteria described above.

The applicant pool is very large and contains every possible combination of skill scores. What is the maximum number of candidates Yessine can accept while ensuring no candidate is more skilled than another?
Since the answer can be large, output it modulo M=998244353%%ZSMJ8%%.
input: The single line of the input contains two space separated integers:
n (1≤n≤103)%%ZSMJ9%% — The number of skills
m (1≤m≤103)%%ZSMJ10%% — The highest possible proficiency score for each skill.
output: Output one integer, representing the desired answer modulo 998244353%%ZSMJ11%%
